detail.abstract:
Estimates of Australian photovoltaic (PV) waste vary considerably, but all point to substantial and rapidly growing volumes over the coming decade, placing increasing demand on downstream end-of-life (EOL) infrastructure. 

Existing research has predominantly addressed technical recycling feasibility, material recovery and individual policy mechanisms, giving comparatively less attention to the cross-domain interfaces and interdependencies among the technical, governance, economic and reverselogistics conditions that determine whether EOL materials can move through coordinated recovery pathways and re-enter productive use. This paper addresses these interactions by developing a four-gap typology comprising interacting technical, governance, economic and reverse-logistics gaps that can inhibit material loop closure in Australian PV EOL management. The typology is developed through an integrative literature synthesis, informed by a Systems-of-Systems (SoS) perspective, and is illustrated using two structurally distinct Australian PV EOL environments: the remote context of Uterne Solar Farm in the Northern Territory (NT), and the utility-scale, National Electricity Market (NEM)-connected context of Metz Solar Farm in New South Wales (NSW). These environments are used as structural illustrations in site application rather than as like-for-like comparative case studies. The analysis finds that loop closure cannot be explained by a single technical, policy, economic or logistical deficiency; the four gap dimensions interact to produce structural disconnections between material recovery, decisionmaking, economic incentives and reverse-logistics pathways, locating PV EOL vulnerabilities at the level of systems architecture and interfaces with limited public information compounding all four.

detail.abstract: Maintenance restores equipment performance, yet the intervention itself can introduce defects that are discovered only after restart. Wrong components, incomplete isolation, incorrect settings, omitted fasteners and ineffective functional tests can arise through interactions among task design, work environment, supervision and organisational constraints. This conceptual paper proposes a risk-based framework for reducing such maintenanceinduced failures in industrial equipment. A focused synthesis of human reliability analysis, maintenance error taxonomies, systems safety and reliability engineering informs six connected stages: define the intervention and operating state; decompose failure-sensitive tasks; identify error mechanisms and performance-shaping conditions; prioritise credible equipment consequences; apply layered preventive and recovery controls; and verify performance after release with feedback into work planning. The proposed decision unit is the maintenance task and its affected equipment function, rather than a generic worker error score. Human error probabilities, where used, are treated as uncertain, context-dependent inputs; the framework does not infer a universal rate. Three tables compare methods, map risk factors to controls and specify evidence at each decision stage. Two figures are reproduced from separate peer-reviewed open-access studies with explicit attribution: one presents the distribution of published electrical-maintenance outage events, and the other maps factors influencing errors in mining-truck maintenance. Their case data and models belong to the original authors and do not validate this paper. The contribution is a testable architecture connecting task risk to post-maintenance functional assurance, management responsibility and learning. Future studies should evaluate induced-defect rates, near misses, independent verification quality and equipment outcomes across different maintenance contexts. No original dataset, experiment, survey or deployment is claimed.

detail.abstract: Offshore wind is expanding rapidly to meet net-zero targets, but whether it has been sited to avoid impacts to marine biodiversity remains unclear. We present a global assessment of overlap between offshore wind and globally recognized important biodiversity features (marine protected areas (MPA), key biodiversity areas (KBA), ecologically or biologically significant areas (EBSA), and marine wilderness), quantifying overlap and testing whether siting differs from random expectations. Globally, 21.2% of offshore wind structures fell within at least one biodiversity feature, most often MPAs (17.5%) and KBAs (6.4%); a 25 km buffer raised exposure to over 22,580 km² for KBAs and 55,510 km² for MPAs. Siting rarely differed from random expectations, with only two countries showing lower and three greater-than-expected overlap. As offshore wind scales up, embedding biodiversity impact avoidance into early-stage marine spatial planning will be critical for reconciling the clean energy transition with global biodiversity goals.

detail.abstract: The deliberate destruction of the nation's most revered symbol puts the First Amendment to its most crucial test. This unconventional scholarly paper, written in verse, examines the constitutional protection of flag burning. Its primary doctrinal focus is on the facts, holding, and reasoning of Texas v. Johnson, positioning that case within the broader political speech tradition, extending from West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette's prohibition on compelled patriotic orthodoxy to the Court's protection of offensive symbolic expression. It argues that the Supreme Court got it correct: the government may neither compel reverence for a national symbol nor suppress its desecration merely because the message conveyed is deeply offensive to the majority. The paper also highlights a recurring paradox of First Amendment law, which is that constitutional protection is often most critical precisely when the expression at issue is widely despised. Though written in verse, the paper is grounded in judicial decisions, historical sources, public opinion evidence, and legal scholarship. The paper uses an unconventional scholarly form to examine a foundational constitutional proposition, that the freedom to dissent from national orthodoxy necessarily includes the freedom to reject, deface, and even destroy the symbols through which that orthodoxy is expressed.

detail.abstract: In recent decades, there has been a noticeable upward trajectory in the frequency of automotive recalls. These recalls endure significant delays, posing a threat to the number of vehicles recalled being effectively addressed and, in turn, contributing to injuries and fatalities. Extant research has concentrated on examining recalls from a manufacturer's vantage point, overlooking the NHTSA process that can facilitate/dictate recalls. These studies have identified factors at the individual level (e.g., compensation structure), organizational level (e.g., plant utilization), and recall-specific factors (e.g., identification of the problem's source) that can facilitate prompt recalls but they overlook the insightful role of owners' complaints, which are reported well in advance of official recall announcements. The acquisition of insights from these owners' complaints emerges as a crucial aspect to facilitate the NHTSA recall investigation process and proactively initiate recalls. We utilize the theoretical lens of Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) to develop a recall prediction system based on a deep learning, natural language processing (NLP) model called Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). We analyze a substantial dataset of complaints, and our study provides promising insights, predicting a recall with an F1-score of 0.9 even 5 months before the concerned authority issues it. Additionally, we empirically demonstrate the social benefit of recalling early. We deploy a different data set for robustness and the results are remarkably consistent. Our approach also contributes to a broader comprehension of recall dynamics within the automotive industry. Ultimately, this knowledge can inform theoretical perspectives, practical applications, and policymaking efforts.

detail.abstract: Circular plastic supply chains must decide where to process dispersed post-consumer material and how to govern the quality-improving investments of recovery facilities and processors. We model governance-spot exchange, linear contract, joint venture (JV), or ownership by either party-as an allocation of marginal claims over jointly created value. The claim a mode can implement determines equilibrium sorting and processing investment and hence the usable fraction of every gross ton. A JV differs from a contract because a separate legal entity makes otherwise commingled residual value verifiable and divisible. We embed this mechanism in a capacitated, multi-resin facility-location model calibrated to 32,793 U.S. ZIP codes and 203 plastic recyclers, in which sites, governance by site and resin, spec-grade blending, and flows are chosen jointly. In this calibrated design study, governance is the most consequential decision in every scenario, ahead of plural governance and siting. Relative to uniform spot exchange, optimized governance raises value added by 6-11% when arm's-length quality meets specifications and by 30% or more when it does not. Plural governance beats the best uniform mode by 0.7-3.3%, and locating sites before choosing governance loses 0-2.3%, or 5.7% under strict specifications. JVs are chosen only where complementary, nonverifiable investments meet binding specifications at high-volume sites. Under simulated lot-level quality, designs planned on expected quality miss specifications on 14-36% of spec-grade tons, and a small quality margin raises realized value in every case. Governance parameters are varied transparently rather than estimated, so the results are conditional design prescriptions.

detail.abstract: National AI policy documents are often compared by what they mention. A strategy that names transparency, fairness and accountability looks complete, even if no sentence in it requires anyone to do anything. This paper asks whether a reproducible, citation-grounded procedure can separate what a policy document mentions from what it requires. We describe Meridian, a method that reads every operative sentence of a supplied document set and places it on a five-step normative-force ladder (aspirational, intentional, assigned, obligatory, enforceable), based on its addressee, modal force and any attached consequence. Two indices are kept apart: breadth, the share of 45 expected governance mechanisms a document establishes, and force, the share of those mechanisms carried by binding provisions. Verdicts are computed by rules; a language model writes explanations, and every citation is checked against the source text. We apply the method to stored analyses of 18 instruments from eight jurisdictions: China, Egypt, the European Union, India, Japan, Kenya, Rwanda and the United Kingdom. Breadth and force diverge sharply. Egypt's guidelines reach 84 per cent breadth with no binding mechanism, while China's measures reach 18 per cent breadth with three-quarters of it binding. No jurisdiction binds any environmental-sustainability mechanism. Checking the verdicts against the documents shows errors in both directions: rights-conferring and passive-voice statutory duties are under-read, and "must"-heavy guidance and translated legal idioms are over-read. The method is an early prototype; it has not been validated by legal experts, and the sample is small and exploratory.

detail.abstract: Mathematics learning planning plays a strategic role in determining instructional quality and the achievement of learning objectives. However, teachers encounter various problematics that hinder effective planning. This study aims to identify and analyze these problematics through a systematic literature review of relevant national and international research. The analysis is organized into five dimensions. First, the analysis of student characteristics and needs reveals challenges posed by differences in prior ability, interest, motivation, and learning styles, particularly when diagnostic data are limited. Second, the formulation of learning objectives exposes difficulties in translating general outcomes into specific, measurable objectives and aligning them with students' abilities and materials. Third, the selection of models, methods, and strategies highlights incompatibilities with material characteristics, student development levels, and time constraints. Fourth, the development of teaching materials, media, and resources faces obstacles concerning limited accessible resources and unequal digital technology utilization. Fifth, assessment planning addresses difficulties in selecting techniques, aligning instruments with objectives, incorporating higherorder thinking skills items, and determining success indicators. The findings indicate that these problematics are interrelated, stemming from teacher-related factors and systemic constraints. This study recommends strengthening teacher competencies and institutional support to create more adaptive, inclusive, and effective mathematics learning planning.

detail.abstract: Technical standards occupy a central position in the European Union's approach to trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), including the implementation of regulatory requirements under the EU AI Act through technical and organisational specifications. Their expanding role raises a fundamental question: What can standards legitimately be trusted to establish in public-sector AI implementation? This research essay examines standards both as instruments for supporting trust in AI and as objects of trust whose authority depends on the expertise, institutional arrangements and interests involved in their production. It draws on relevant literature and five purposively selected semi-structured expert interviews covering European and international standardisation as well as local and regional public-administration contexts. The analysis develops three propositions. First, standards can structure the operationalisation of trustworthiness but cannot resolve the normative choices underlying concepts such as fairness, transparency and acceptable risk. Second, their legitimacy and implementability depend on representative participation, transparency and the inclusion of situated public-administration knowledge. Third, standards cannot substitute for the cognitive, organisational and technological agency required to interpret requirements, select appropriate technologies and manage dependencies. The essay concludes that standards can support responsible and innovative AI implementation only where their technical boundaries, institutional legitimacy and relationship to public-administration capacity are explicitly recognised.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates states' SNAP financial obligations under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act through FY2034 using data through FY2025. Annual additional obligations reach $17 billion under constant payment error rates and $13.3 billion under administrative improvement through half convergence. Recession scenarios raise obligations to $17.8-$27 billion. In addition, we find variations in financing with and without the cost shift relative to states’ general-fund revenue. The findings suggest that OBBBA may increase state accountability through a financing schedule that produces uneven burdens, discontinuous incentives, and pro-cyclical fiscal pressure. detail.abstract: We study noncooperative multi-vehicle games among heterogeneous autonomous vehicles, where each vehicle adopts a decentralized closed-loop policy based on its own state, and optimizes an objective that depends on other vehicles through potentially asymmetric interaction weights. We develop an α-potential game framework that reduces the computation of an approximate Nash equilibrium (NE) to the minimization of a single auxiliary α-potential function. We explicitly construct this α-potential, establish the existence of its minimizers, and characterize the equilibrium approximation error α in terms of interaction asymmetry. We further introduce vehicle-specific scaling to reduce the effective interaction asymmetry, thereby tightening the equilibrium approximation and, in important cases, recovering an exact NE despite asymmetric interactions. We also derive social-efficiency guarantees for the potential-selected policies, revealing how the interaction structure shapes worst-case efficiency. Numerical experiments demonstrate the flexibility of the framework in capturing heterogeneous vehicle interactions, collision and obstacle avoidance, lane changing and overtaking under different traffic configurations, and priority-based intersection crossing.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how uncertainty about return-predictive models affects variance bounds on stochastic discount factors (SDFs). We derive an optimally scaled bound from effective conditional moments that combine average within-model risk and disagreement across conditional mean forecasts. Holding the averaged mean and within-model risk fixed, disagreement weakens the bound. Empirically, conditioning information tightens SDF volatility requirements most at the 1-quarter and 1-year horizons. Long-run risk SDFs exhibit finite-sample shortfalls. Raredisaster and habit SDFs clear long-horizon bounds in long simulations, but their finite-sample performance remains uneven. Counterfactuals point to realized disasters and multi-period duration as important for the stronger 5-year disaster-model result; higher risk aversion alone does not resolve shorter-horizon gaps. The framework links predictive-model uncertainty to horizon-specific economic diagnostics while retaining the interpretation of variance bounds as necessary conditions for asset pricing.

detail.abstract: Mathematics learning in schools continues to face various challenges that affect the quality of the learning process and the achievement of educational objectives. This study aims to examine the problematics encountered in the implementation of mathematics learning through a literature review of relevant research findings. The analysis identifies five main categories of problematics: (1) students' understanding of mathematical concepts, including difficulties in abstract reasoning, connecting concepts to everyday life, and using symbols, formulas, and procedures appropriately, which may develop into misconceptions; (2) motivation and interest in learning mathematics, encompassing students' perceptions of mathematics as a difficult subject, low learning interest, lack of self-confidence, and mathematics anxiety; (3) learning strategies and methods, comprising limited variation in teaching methods, teacher-centered learning, inappropriate selection of methods relative to material characteristics, and low student engagement; (4) the use of media and technology, including limited availability of instructional media and teaching aids, suboptimal technology utilization, inadequate facilities, and teachers' limited competence in developing and applying technology-based media; and (5) evaluation and assessment, covering the tendency to emphasize final learning outcomes, insufficient measurement of conceptual understanding, limited variation in test formats, and suboptimal provision of feedback. These findings indicate that the problematics in mathematics learning are interrelated and multidimensional, spanning cognitive, affective, pedagogical, infrastructural, and assessment aspects. Therefore, comprehensive and systematic efforts are required from teachers, schools, and educational stakeholders to address these problematics in order to create meaningful, engaging, and effective mathematics learning.

detail.abstract: Gender equality and workplace inclusivity are essential in promoting fair, respectful, and supportive work environments where employees are provided with equal opportunities and encouraged to participate and contribute. This study aimed to determine the perceived levels of gender equality and workplace inclusivity among employees of a Philippine government agency. A quantitative descriptive-correlational research design was employed using a census approach involving 40 government employees. Data were gathered through a validated and reliable researcher-developed questionnaire that measured gender equality in terms of equal opportunities and fair treatment, workplace inclusivity in terms of respect and acceptance, participation and involvement, and organizational support, as well as workplace policy and practice gaps. Descriptive and inferential statistical techniques were utilized in analyzing the data. Results revealed that employees perceived high levels of gender equality and workplace inclusivity in the workplace. A significant positive relationship was found between gender equality and workplace inclusivity, indicating that employees who perceived higher levels of equal opportunities and fair treatment also tended to perceive higher levels of respect, acc eptance, participation, involvement, and organizational support. Although respondents generally perceived limited workplace policy and practice gaps, areas requiring continuous improvement were identified in accountability and monitoring mechanisms, program evaluation processes, organizational support systems, employee feedback utilization, and safe reporting procedures. Based on these findings, a strategy roadmap for strengthening gender equality and workplace inclusivity was prepared to support the continuous enhancement of gender-responsive and inclusive workplace practices. The findings may serve as a basis for government leaders, human resource managers, and gender and development focal persons in formulating and enhancing evidence-based policies, programs, and interventions that promote gender equality, workplace inclusivity, employee well-being, and organizational effectiveness.

detail.abstract: Two-dimensional material interfaces govern the transfer and conversion of heat, charge, light, ions, molecules, and mechanical stress in emerging energy harvesters. Their role extends from atomic bonding and band alignment to flake junctions, electrode contacts, encapsulation, power conditioning, storage, and system integration. This critical technical review synthesizes interface engineering across thermoelectric, piezoelectric, triboelectric, photovoltaic, thermogalvanic, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and hybrid harvesting technologies. It centers on graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, transition-metal dichalcogenides, black phosphorus, MXenes, and van der Waals heterostructures, while considering nanowires, polymers, quantum dots, and nanostructured thermoelectrics as complementary hybrid components. Evidence shows that interfaces can scatter phonons selectively, separate photocarriers, transfer mechanical stress, tune contact electrification, improve catalytic activity, and connect porous networks. The same interfaces can create electrical and thermal resistance, recombination, charge leakage, delamination, wear, oxidation, side reactions, and manufacturing variability. Device output is further limited by impedance mismatch, rectification, storage loss, parasitic power, source intermittency, and package degradation. The paper proposes the HARVEST framework: Harmonize service and source; Assign each interface a transport function; Resolve coupled carriers and failure modes; Validate the integrated conversion chain; Engineer scalable contacts and packaging; Stress-test reliability and safety; and Track lifecycle energy, resources, and recovery. HARVEST is an evidence-derived framework rather than an experimentally validated model. It links nanoscale interface design to stable conditioned power and sustainable system service.

detail.abstract: The increasing heterogeneity, dynamism, and service diversity of fifth-generation (5G) and emerging sixth-generation (6G) networks create substantial challenges for intelligent resource allocation. Network slices, vehicular applications, edge intelligence, digital twins, multimedia services, and critical communications require resource-management mechanisms capable of responding to changing traffic and Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. This paper examines the role of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in intelligent network resource allocation, with particular methodological attention to the Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MA-DDPG) framework developed by Onaji et al. (2025). The study adopts a literature-based analytical synthesis, distinguishing the simulation methodology and empirical findings of the primary reference from the findings reported by other supplied studies. The literature indicates a progression from conventional optimization and heuristic allocation toward adaptive, distributed, and learning-based control. The primary study demonstrates this transition through a cooperative multiagent architecture using Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), continuous action spaces, multiobjective reward design, and a custom discrete-event network-slicing simulator. Other studies extend intelligent allocation toward hierarchical RAN slicing, federated learning, secure spectrum management, vehicular networks, edge intelligence, task offloading, digital twins, and decentralized 6G control. Building on this evidence, the paper proposes a literature-grounded framework in which DRL integrates network-state observation, adaptive resource decisions, QoS-aware reward mechanisms, multi-agent coordination, and continuous feedback. The framework is conceptual and is not presented as independently validated by the present study.

detail.abstract: We study liquidity and price discovery on Polymarket using complete on-chain trades and tick-level top-of-book quotes. Spreads are tightest and books deepest near $0 and $1, and widest and thinnest around $0.50. No trade occurs in 99% of one-minute intervals, yet they account for 76% of price variation. A vector autoregression attributes at most 4% of efficient-price innovation variance to trades, with quote updates driving several times more price discovery. Midquotes are accurate forecasts when spreads are tight and a recent trade is marginally more accurate, but most markets have little to no trading and trade's accuracy worsens in staleness.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence automates outcome production and widens competitive asymmetries, social external rewards (status, recognition, economic return) become rarer and more unevenly distributed. I argue that this structural shift creates a systemic decline in the reliability of outcome-based positive feedback loops that historically sustained large portions of human motivation. Drawing on economics, psychology, neuroscience, and existential philosophy, I develop a formal model that (1) characterizes the dynamics of external vs. intrinsic reinforcement under rising substitutability, (2) identifies the conditions under which a transition to process-oriented, self-driven feedback is not only adaptive but necessary, and (3) describes psychological obstacles, design strategies, and societal trade-offs of such a transition. I propose a concrete micro-reinforcement architecture-Continuous Micro-Reinforcement (CMR)-and recommend empirical tests. The central normative claim: in highly automatable domains, value should be reconceptualized primarily in terms of subjective experience and social sharing of process (rather than purely objective, outcome-based merit), while accepting a pluralistic, division-of-labor society in which AI handles large outcome-production tasks and humans orient to intrinsically meaningful processes.

detail.abstract: Trade restrictions intended to address environmental externalities can also distort production by limiting access to imported inputs. We examine this tradeoff using China's 2017 waste import ban. Combining rich data from multiple sources, we exploit variation in pre-ban import exposure across cities and firms. Although the ban reduces satellite-detected dumping-site area and waste-sector methane emissions in exposed cities, it induces contrasting adjustments along the supply chain. Entry shifts toward collectors in small recycling markets and away from manufacturing-capable recyclers in large ones. Entry also declines in downstream industries using restricted materials. Incumbent firms holding pre-ban waste-import licenses scale down operations.

detail.abstract: Human resource (HR) training and development are now viewed as strategic instruments, but in practice, training is often implemented without a thorough needs analysis, and any performance issues are easily addressed with training. This article aims to outline the diagnosis of HR training and development needs through a literature review. The discussion includes training from a strategic perspective, training needs assessment (TNA), performance gap and competency gap analysis, the differences between the two in determining the need for training, root cause analysis (RCA), data triangulation, transforming business gaps into learning needs, stakeholder collaboration, and reskilling and upskilling in the era of artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalization. The study results indicate that a performance gap does not automatically indicate a need for training. Training is necessary if the diagnosis proves that the primary cause of the gap is a lack of knowledge or skills that can be addressed through learning, while other causes, such as systems, equipment, work procedures, feedback, and motivation, are addressed through non-training interventions. RCA and data triangulation complement each other in examining the causes of gaps, while stakeholder collaboration helps prioritize needs. A systematic needs diagnosis is the basis for ensuring that training is on target, aligned with organizational strategy, and relevant to changing skills needs.

detail.abstract: The Raxaul-Amlekhganj Railway, opened in 1927, was the principal southern rail connection of the Nepal Government Railway and an early attempt to solve a structural problem of Nepalese statecraft: how to connect a landlocked, mountainous capital and its markets to the railway network of British India. This case study treats the railway not only as transport technology but as a state institution embedded in the Rana political order, the political transition of 1950-51, the emergence of development planning, the opening of labour organisation, and the subsequent prioritisation of roads and aviation. It reconstructs the railway's operating model, supply-chain role, workforce, technical constraints, commercial performance and decline, then follows its institutional afterlife through rehabilitation proposals, the persistence of the Raxaul-Birgunj gateway and later cross-border railway planning. The central conclusion is deliberately analytical rather than normative: the NGR illustrates how infrastructure performance is produced by the interaction of technology, geography, network design, organisational capacity, maintenance, labour, fiscal priorities and competing transport systems.

detail.abstract: Offshore wind expansion is central to achieving net-zero emissions but risks exacerbating biodiversity loss if poorly planned. Biodiversity impact avoidance offers the most effective pathway to reconcile development with conservation, but its application in offshore wind remains unclear. Here, we reviewed offshore wind siting policies across 28 jurisdictions to evaluate how biodiversity impact avoidance is embedded in planning frameworks. We found that 71% of jurisdictions explicitly excluded at least one biodiversity feature from site selection, but exclusions were narrow, inconsistent, and largely limited to protected areas. A global spatial analysis of offshore wind infrastructure and marine protected areas revealed substantial overlap even where exclusions applied. These findings reveal a critical implementation gap in the mitigation hierarchy: failure to avoid impacts early risks shifting unrealistic expectations onto minimization, restoration, and offsetting-approaches that are particularly uncertain in marine systems. Strengthening biodiversity impact avoidance could improve outcomes for both climate and biodiversity.

detail.abstract: In this study, I look at whether the logistics performance of the leading economies remains stable over time. Since transport and logistics are of great importance for trade, only a small number of studies have tracked the same group of top countries in each edition of the World Bank Logistics Performance Index (LPI), including the 2023 edition which followed the period of the COVID-19 pandemic. I have used secondary data, consisting of the overall LPI scores for 12 high-income economies across seven editions (2007, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2023). I analyzed the average score of the group, the changes in each economy's score between editions, the shifts in their rankings, and the amount by which each economy's score increased or decreased. The findings indicate that the average score of the group was almost identical in 2007 (4.01), in 2018 (4.00) and in 2023 (4.04). Between 2018 and 2023 six economies improved while six declined. A high score in 2018 did not ensure a high score in 2023 and the rankings changed significantly: Canada advanced by 13 places whereas the United Kingdom dropped by 10. Japan had the most stable scores and Finland and Austria the least stable. The results demonstrate that holding a top position in the LPI does not guarantee a future top position. However, the sample is small and the 2023 scores are rounded, so the conclusions have to be treated with caution.

detail.abstract: We introduce a metric for detecting liquidity void (LVD) events-sudden, large withdrawals of resting depth from the top of the limit order book-and characterize their post-event price dynamics. Using one month each of ETHUSDT (August 2026) and BTCUSDT (June 2026) spot order book data (2.85 million reconstructed snapshots, 745,000 detected LVD events), we document three findings. First, LVD events are followed by positive mean reversion in both assets at every horizon. Under standard errors clustered by hour, this effect is statistically significant at short-tomedium horizons (up to 10 seconds) in all four asset-side combinations, and at every horizon for ETHUSDT bid-side events. Second, the effect is conditional on the structural significance of the void. Segmenting events into terciles of the void side's pre-event share of total depth produces a monotone pattern in both assets: voids on the thin side produce strong mean reversion, while voids on the thick side produce little or none. Third, this conditioning variable reconciles the opposite aggregate asymmetries observed in the two assets, and it replicates out-of-sample in both. The effect survives controls for pre-event spread, volatility, and event magnitude in a regression on 356,777 ETHUSDT events with Newey-West HAC standard errors. We do not find that the effect is tradeable as a standalone strategy, nor that gating execution on LVD events improves implementation shortfall.

detail.abstract: Management theories develop from organizational worlds shaped by prevailing technologies. Those technologies affect not only what organizations do but also which organizational configurations scholars can routinely observe. We call a feature of a technological regime that materially restricts such configurations a technological support condition. Technological support conditions are one class of feasibility constraints, but they warrant separate attention because regime change can relax them quickly enough to populate previously sparse organizational states within observable historical time. When restricted variation leaves analytically distinct mechanisms bundled in a target theoretical literature, we call the result theory compression. We develop state-space problematization as a six-test procedure requiring analytic separability, a prior feasibility constraint, compression in a defensibly bounded target literature, newly occupied variation, mechanism relevance, and rival-change discipline. We demonstrate the approach through organizational control and apply it more briefly to organizational learning. The control application identifies gross adjudication demand relative to reliable evaluative capacity as an independent control-design condition. The learning application separates cumulative individual experience, contemporaneous performance, and assistance-independent capability. Technological change can therefore do more than create new phenomena for theory to explain. It can alter the empirical support against which inherited theories are judged.

title: The Consciousness Exemption ProblemWhy Uncertainty About Machine Sentience Should Increase, Not Decrease, Ethical Scrutiny of AI-Driven Consumption Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.abstract:
Whether current or near-future artificial intelligence systems possess phenomenal consciousness or sentience remains scientifically and philosophically unresolved, a fact openly acknowledged even by the industry laboratories that build these systems. This paper argues that this very uncertainty, far from licensing reduced ethical scrutiny, obligates greater scrutiny of AI systems deployed to shape human consumption behaviour. It introduces the Consciousness Exemption Problem: the tendency in public and industry discourse to treat an AI system's uncertain or absent inner experience as grounds for moral exemption (“it is just a machine, so no real harm is done”), when the same uncertainty, read through a precautionary asymmetry, cuts in the opposite direction.

The argument draws on three bodies of work that have not, to the best of the author's knowledge, previously been brought together. The first is philosophy of mind and the contemporary debate on machine consciousness (Chalmers, Nagel, Searle, McClelland, Birch). The second is consumption economics and social psychology (Veblen, Duesenberry, Festinger), which document replicable and therefore exploitable human decision patterns such as status-signalling consumption and social comparison. The third is a phenomenological and hermeneutic account, developed through a limited method of reflective observation and two illustrative cases, of how human meaning is actively reconstructed by consciousness rather than retrieved as fixed data. A two-tier conceptual model separates computable cognition (Tier 1), where AI capability is extensively demonstrated, from phenomenal consciousness or sentience (Tier 2), where it is genuinely uncertain. The central claim does not require Tier 2 to be empty; it requires only that its status be uncertain.

The argument is illustrated through AI-optimised marketing and recommendation systems, which detect and amplify known human decision patterns at a scale, level of personalisation and degree of tirelessness that no conscious human persuader could sustain, and without any verified internal moderating friction (empathy, fatigue, guilt, felt consequence) of the kind that constrains a human actor engaged in comparable conduct. Global advertising expenditure (approximately US$384 billion in 2011 and US$1.14 trillion in 2025) and global anxiety and depression prevalence data are presented strictly as corroborating context, not causal proof. The paper identifies an industry asymmetry, in which epistemic humility about the possible inner states of AI systems coexists with epistemic complacency about their demonstrated persuasive effects on humans, and it analyses the role of motivated ambiguity in sustaining that asymmetry.

The paper anticipates and rebuts six objections, including the functionalist claim that consciousness is a distraction from designer responsibility. It concludes that governance and design frameworks should treat sentience uncertainty as an aggravating factor that triggers externally imposed safeguards, including disclosure of psychological targeting, limits on the intensity of personalised persuasion, independent audit, and a rule against strategic ambiguity about sentience claims, rather than as reassurance that no genuine harm is possible. The paper is a philosophical argument rather than a causal study, and it closes by identifying survey- and interview-based research that could test its phenomenological claims.

title: The Moving Boundary of Production: Constraint Migration and Institutional Inertia

detail.abstract:
Development policy often begins with a list of deficiencies: infrastructure, finance, skills, technology, institutions, exports, or demand. This paper argues that the more useful question is not which deficiencies exist, but which margin currently constrains the reproduction or expansion of productive activity.

The paper defines the boundary of production as the currently binding margin beyond which additional productive activity becomes disproportionately difficult. The boundary is not fixed. Successful development changes it. Transport scarcity can give way to power scarcity; finance can become more important after physical bottlenecks are relaxed; skilled labour can become binding after investment accelerates; and a system that once lacked productive capacity can later face weak demand, profitability, or other limits to further expansion.

The paper develops constraint migration as the general process and constraint inversion as a narrower possibility. Constraint inversion occurs when organisational capabilities built to solve an earlier bottleneck remain concentrated on that margin after the principal constraint has moved elsewhere. The problem is therefore not institutional weakness but misalignment between institutional strength and the current production boundary.

The framework requires independent identification. Constraints should be inferred from observable shortages, shadow costs, delays, utilisation patterns, rejected orders, substitution behaviour, and other evidence rather than from the policy response itself. This produces a comparative and historical research strategy for studying how successful productive systems generate new constraints and how organisations adapt‑‑or fail to adapt‑‑as the boundary moves.

detail.abstract: Should a state let a new activity grow before building the rules that govern it, or build the rules first? Governments face this choice with digital payments, cryptoassets, online platforms and artificial intelligence, and usually answer it by doctrine: "growth first" or "governance first". We develop a framework that replaces doctrine with diagnosis. Three forces, studied in separate literatures, each enter in their own way. Waiting lets the state learn which rules work. Ungoverned activity causes harm that can persist long after rules arrive. Without coordination, activity is both smaller and slower-growing. The cost of governing also changes over time, falling as the state builds capacity and rising as private interests entrench. We find that how long harm lasts matters as much as how large it is, and that coordination favours early governance because waiting forgoes growth. When entrenchment grows with the size of an industry, sectors polarise, and in the limit the reason to wait disappears: the only question is whether governing pays at today's cost. A regulator who ignores entrenchment governs too late, and possibly never. Uncertainty about how large a sector will become differs from uncertainty about how to govern it. Only the latter justifies waiting, and only if the market reveals the right rules faster than a hurdle that rises with the persistence of harm. When larger markets teach faster, the best time to govern can be a window rather than a single threshold, giving formal content to the Collingridge dilemma. Illustrative exercises show that uniform doctrines are costly, and we draw policy lessons for regulators, developing economies and those governing new technologies.

title: Projects without Production Systems: Administrative Legibility and Organisational Failure

detail.abstract:
Development interventions are often organised as projects because projects are governable. They have budgets, contractors, schedules, deliverables, completion dates, and identifiable responsibility. Production systems are harder to administer because many of their essential capabilities emerge through repeated operation: maintenance routines, supplier formation, labour mobility, financing relationships, technical learning, and adaptation.

This paper develops the concept of administrative legibility bias: the tendency of governments, lenders, donors, and other funding organisations to favour interventions whose boundaries and outputs can be specified in advance. The bias is not evidence of poor administration. It can arise from ordinary requirements of budgeting, contracting, auditing, accountability, and risk allocation. The problem appears when project completion is treated as evidence of system formation.

A limiting case makes the distinction clear. A factory, industrial park, or infrastructure asset can be delivered on time, on budget, and to engineering specification while the surrounding production system remains thin. The paper therefore separates project performance from productive-system formation and proposes post-completion tests based on utilisation, local interdependence, reproduction, and adaptation.

The argument is conditional rather than anti-project. Projects can anchor industrial development. The relevant question is what productive relationships continue to form after formal delivery, and whether evaluation systems can observe those relationships before declaring developmental completion.

detail.abstract: We study how the market for used capital finances entry into a more productive sector under financial frictions. We develop analytical and quantitative general equilibrium models with heterogeneous producers, markets for new and used capital, collateral constraints, and fixed costs of entry. Used capital has a higher user cost but requires a lower down payment than new capital, making it easier to finance. This financing advantage allows producers with limited net worth to enter the productive sector even when entry using new capital alone is not worthwhile. We analytically show that access to used capital lowers the entry threshold and that this threshold falls as the price of used capital declines. In the calibrated dynamic model, access to used capital raises TFP by 14.8%, with entry accounting for 88.5% of the TFP gain.

detail.abstract: Most of what humanity builds, decides and produces requires a transformation, in which talent, resources and demand become coordinated action and value. When many heterogeneous elements sustain that transformation to one end, and keep it up over time, it acquires a collective form, and this paper starts from the hypothesis that the form is the organization. Organizational research describes organizations with exceptional precision through what they contain, and has yet to define, in terms that generate testable consequences, the form itself, which persists when the parts are replaced and can stop acting as one while every part remains. The paper proposes a construct for it, the organizational regime, which represents the relations through which the transformation acquires, reproduces and changes its form. The regime is drawn on four coupled dimensions, field, structure, energetics and context, and observed through people, assets, leadership and mission. A candidate mechanism, the element pathway, specifies how elements enter the regime and take part in it through access, activation, alignment, organizational weight and uptake capacity, and eight propositions followfive from the pathway and three on how the regime itself changes. Before any physics enters, and drawing only on what is established about organizations, the paper derives three requirements a theory of the organization as a generated form must satisfy. It must explain how elements of comparable position come to differ in their capacity to shape collective action, how distributed potential becomes coordinated activity, and how the resulting form persists, transforms and follows a trajectory. The reference system is the tropical cyclone, a form of this kind that physics understands in depth, and it answers the second. An organization requires the other two as well, so the framework extends the cyclone in both directions. It reaches backward to field theory, where an element's effective properties arise from its coupling to a field, and forward to complex-systems dynamics, where a form persists, transforms and follows a trajectory in a state space. The three compose one architecture. From each, the framework transfers the structure of relations, one relation at a time. Where a relation holds, an organizational magnitude is expected to stand in for each physical one and the relation may keep its mathematical form. The formulas themselves never travel, and every relation remains a hypothesis to be retained, adapted or rejected. Whatever an organization requires beyond this architecture has to enter through some physics or be shown to emerge from the relations of the system, and what does neither marks a boundary of the framework. Candidate measures for each construct, and an illustrative reading of the history of one company, Patagonia, Inc., as a chain of field transitions, show what the framework makes visible. The paper closes with what would falsify the framework, what a test would require, and the questions the framework opens beyond the single organization, among them interacting regimes, populations of regimes and why organizations exist at all.

detail.abstract: This article examines the commonly taught belief that the American flag must always be physically higher than accompanying Colors in a military color guard. Through a comparative doctrinal analysis of Army TC 3-21.5, Marine Corps Order 5060.20, and Department of the Air Force Pamphlet 34-1203, the paper distinguishes ceremonial precedence and position of honor from physical flag height. It demonstrates that Army doctrine prescribes equal finial height at the Carry, Marine Corps doctrine establishes equal height as the intended configuration while permitting the national Colors to be slightly higher when equality cannot be achieved, and Department of the Air Force procedures examined do not prescribe a specific relative-height relationship. The article argues that position of honor is expressed through multiple mechanisms, including formation position, bearer seniority, command authority, saluting conventions, and context-specific display requirements. In doing so, it separates formal doctrine from instructional shorthand and provides a more precise framework for understanding how national precedence is represented within military color guard procedures.

detail.abstract: Intraday "scalping" of index derivatives is popular among Indian retail traders, yet the market regulator reports that most individual derivatives traders lose money. This paper reviews a small, purposively selected body of evidence on one question: under what conditions can a short-horizon strategy on Nifty derivatives earn a positive net return, and who is likely to earn it? We synthesise (i) a cost-aware study of simple intraday rules on S&P 500 futures, (ii) two working papers on high-frequency trader (HFT) behaviour on Indian exchanges, (iii) a recent article on intraday volatility on the National Stock Exchange (NSE), (iv) the Securities and Exchange Board of India's (SEBI) FY2025-26 studies of individual derivatives traders, and (v) the 2025-26 changes to the retail algorithmic-trading framework and to securities transaction tax (STT). Three themes emerge. First, transaction costs, rather than signal quality, usually decide whether a scalping rule survives. Second, profits in Indian derivatives are concentrated among algorithmic participants, although the regulator's definition of an "algo entity" is broad. Third, backtests of short-horizon strategies are fragile to fill assumptions, regime change and over-fitting. We add a simple breakeven calculation showing that the April 2026 STT increase more than doubled the all-in index-point hurdle for a Nifty futures round trip in an illustrative case, and we state five testable propositions. This is a narrative review and presents no new empirical results.

detail.abstract: Assessment and evaluation in mathematics learning function not merely to measure outcomes but also to diagnose needs, provide feedback, and improve instructional quality. Their implementation, however, faces complex problems across stages: instrument design (misalignment with objectives, dominance of routine problems, limited HOTS items, low validity and reliability), implementation (time constraints, diverse student characteristics, mathematics anxiety, low motivation, technological constraints), and scoring and interpretation (subjectivity, inconsistent rubrics, suboptimal use of results). Addressing these problems requires systematic efforts, including developing valid and reliable instruments, aligning assessment with objectives, providing constructive feedback, utilizing results for remedial and enrichment, enhancing teacher competence, and integrating technology appropriately. Effective, fair, and sustainable mathematics assessment thus demands a comprehensive, continuous approach oriented toward improving learning quality rather than merely assigning grades.

detail.abstract:
The campaign against the trafficking of women and girls at the turn of the twentieth century represented an important stage in the development of international approaches to human trafficking. In Britain, the National Vigilance Association (NVA) became one of the most active organisations involved in this movement. Between 1899 and 1909, the Association expanded its activities beyond domestic moral reform and became closely connected with an emerging international network concerned with what was then described as the "white slave trade." In 1899, the NVA invited representatives from different countries to London for an International Congress on the White Slave Trade, an event that contributed to the establishment of the International Bureau for the Suppression of the White Slave Traffic. The Bureau subsequently worked across national boundaries and encouraged cooperation between voluntary organisations and governments. 

This article examines the international campaign of the National Vigilance Association between 1899 and 1909, with particular attention to its moral reform agenda, international cooperation, relationship with the British state, and understanding of trafficking. It argues that the NVA made significant contributions to the organisation of international anti-trafficking activity, particularly by encouraging communication between reformers, police authorities and governments. At the same time, its campaign was shaped by the moral assumptions of late Victorian and Edwardian Britain. The Association frequently understood sexual exploitation through categories of morality, respectability, gender, class and nationality. Consequently, its campaign contained both humanitarian and paternalistic elements. 

The article therefore treats the NVA neither simply as a successful humanitarian organisation nor as an entirely ineffective moral reform movement. Instead, it examines the contradictions within its work. The Association helped to place trafficking on an international political agenda, but its understanding of the problem was also influenced by contemporary fears about foreigners, prostitution and female sexuality. The period from 1899 to 1909 was therefore important not only because of the practical measures introduced against trafficking, but also because it demonstrated the difficulties involved in defining and addressing exploitation within an international system.

detail.abstract: This study examines the problems associated with the use of media and teaching aids in mathematics learning. Mathematics contains many abstract and symbolic concepts that are often difficult for students to understand through verbal explanation alone. Learning media and teaching aids serve as intermediaries that help visualize abstract concepts into more concrete, observable, and meaningful forms. This study aims to identify the forms of problems, influencing factors, impacts, and strategies to overcome them. The method employed is a literature review by analyzing various relevant sources. The results indicate that the problems include limited availability of media, incompatibility between media and mathematical content, and teachers' difficulties in using technology-based media. Influencing factors comprise teacher competence and skills, creativity and innovation, school support, classroom environment and facilities, and technological developments. The impacts include students' difficulties in understanding concepts, misconceptions, decreased motivation and interest, lack of interaction, and low learning outcomes. Strategies include enhancing teacher competence, increasing creativity in making simple teaching aids, utilizing digital technology, and strengthening school support. This study concludes that the use of media and teaching aids requires synergy between teacher competence, creativity, school support, and appropriate technology integration.

detail.abstract: This study examines the problematics of understanding mathematical concepts among students through a comprehensive literature review of various research findings. The primary objective is to identify and analyze the fundamental issues, indicators, forms, influencing factors, impacts, and efforts to overcome difficulties in comprehending mathematical concepts. The reviewed literature reveals that students' understanding of mathematical concepts often remains superficial, characterized by memorization of formulas and procedures without deep comprehension of underlying meanings. Key problematics identified include: (1) difficulties in explaining, connecting, and applying concepts across different situations; (2) challenges in understanding foundational concepts such as fractions, geometry, algebra, and arithmetic operations; (3) low relational understanding and mathematical connection abilities; (4) inadequate representation skills; and (5) passive learning engagement. Contributing factors encompass internal aspectsincluding initial mathematical ability, self-efficacy, learning interest, motivation, study habits, concentration, and mathematics anxiety-as well as external factors such as teaching methods, instructional media, learning environment, and parental support. The impacts of low conceptual understanding manifest in students' difficulties solving problems, applying concepts to novel situations, and developing logical-mathematical reasoning. The study underscores the necessity of active, contextual, and concrete learning experiences that activate prior knowledge, utilize manipulative aids and technology, connect mathematics to real-life contexts, and foster students' confidence and independence in constructing conceptual understanding. These findings imply that educators should adopt varied instructional approaches tailored to students' characteristics, provide gradual scaffolding, and create supportive learning environments to optimize conceptual understanding in mathematics education.

detail.abstract: Food insecurity is consistently associated with poor health among displaced populations (Gichunge et al., 2020). The Syrian war is one of the most devastating humanitarian crisis in this century (Latschan, 2024). Hunger and malnutrition among Syrian refugees, as well as their health consequences, have received limited attention in the literature. Evidence on the association between recent hunger among adults and general health in a Jordanian refugee cohort also remains limited. We examine this prospective association using data from the Syrian Refugee Life Study. Methods and results The analysis links the 2021 and 2022 interviews and applies a respondent-continuity screen. The primary sample contains 1,969 adults. Ordered-logit models connect any hunger in the preceding seven days at baseline to three-category self-rated health at follow up, adjusting sequentially for baseline health, age, sex and housing characteristics. Baseline hunger was reported by 19.6% of respondents. In the fully adjusted model, hunger was associated with a 3.38 percentage-point higher probability of poor or very poor follow-up health (95% CI 0.95 to 5.80) and a 6.21-point lower probability of good health. Selection weighting and additional controls produced similar estimates, while binary, multinomial and incident-poor-health specifications were less precise. Conclusions Recent hunger identifies adult refugee respondents with a less favourable subsequent health distribution, conditional on measured baseline health and circumstances. The analysis supports a prospective association, but it does not identify a causal effect of hunger or a humanitarian programme.

detail.abstract: Uddin (2026) reports that adding data-driven risk targeting to a 25 percent reallocation of bridge capital toward preventive treatment raises the reduction in cumulative Poor-condition bridge-years from 33.1 to 53.5 percent, but his model charges nothing for building or running the predictive system and assumes it works from year one. This paper asks what the predictive capability is worth net of cost and delay. I extend a reimplementation of his three-state Markov model with an ongoing analytics cost and a one-time build cost, both expressed as shares of the annual capital program, a lag before targeting takes effect, and a rampup period. Value is measured in bridge-years of Poor-condition exposure avoided, so no dollar conversion is needed. Three findings stand out. First, most of the benefit Uddin credits to targeting is available without analytics: when each arm chooses its own best preventive share, the gain from targeting at zero cost falls from 20.3 to 5.4 percent of baseline exposure. Second, the results are sensitive to the cost structure. With re-optimized shares and no lag, targeting stays worthwhile until ongoing costs reach about 18 percent of the annual program, but each year of delay lowers this break-even threshold, which falls to about 8 percent after four years, and, with a lag of one year or more, an upfront build cost of about one quarter of one year's program eliminates the net benefit. Third, the conclusion depends on the time horizon and on assumed cost levels: under lower-cost assumptions (ongoing cost about 1 percent and build cost about 5 percent of a year's program), 99 percent of 400 parameter draws show a positive net benefit with a median of 2.6 percent of baseline exposure, whereas under higher-cost assumptions only 20 percent do, with a median of-3.4 percent. The cost ranges are my assumptions, not evidence; the contribution of the paper is the break-even map that lets an agency compare its own cost estimates against it. All results are properties of a stylized model and do not measure the real value of predictive analytics.

detail.abstract: This paper provides direct empirical insights into the relationship between customer withdrawal behavior and retail food waste. Customers often select the freshest products, leaving earlier-expiring units on the shelf and increasing the risk of those units remaining unsold. Although retailers and researchers widely recognize this mechanism, its magnitude remains insufficiently quantified because systematic shelf-life data are rarely available. Existing insights therefore rely largely on qualitative evidence and theoretical models, making the link between later-expiry withdrawals and retail food waste an important emerging research area. Against this background, we partnered with a leading European grocery retailer to create a novel dataset containing expiry date information at the store-product level. We implemented an adapted data-collection process at a regional warehouse that provided expiry date information for each product delivery entering a store and enabled us to reconstruct expiry-date-specific inventory flows. By combining these data with transactional records for 1, 877 chilled products across 211 stores, we develop a novel and replicable approach for quantifying retail food waste associated with customers' least-expire-first-out withdrawals. Our findings show that, on average, 45% of the retail food waste in our setting is classified as customer-pickingrelated. We further use an exploratory approach to identify product and store characteristics associated with this waste. The results show meaningful associations with (i) store-operational characteristics, including the variety of expiry dates available and the use of expiry-based discounts, and (ii) product characteristics, including retail price and organic status. An additional online experiment shows that higher prices increase customers' search effort. Finally, counterfactual inventory simulations show that strict first-expired-first-out (FEFO) withdrawal reduces expiration waste by 42.0% relative to the observed withdrawal sequence, while more last-expired-first-out (LEFO)-oriented withdrawal increases waste and retailer costs. Overall, the shift from LEFO to FEFO represents a substantial opportunity to improve profitability. In our dynamic simulation, under the most extreme withdrawal comparison, moving from strict LEFO to strict FEFO increases the retailer's margin by almost 2 percentage points, nearly doubling its profitability.

detail.abstract: A new effective date on a mandated price list is often read as evidence of repricing. In 348 audited annual intervals of Greater Austin funeral-home price lists (2013-2024), headline prices changed in 87.2% of intervals with a new date and 32.8% with an unchanged date, and the gap survives removing changes that reverse. detail.abstract: Does centralized pricing require a chain to charge one price? I study itemized prices at multi-establishment funeral providers, a local-service setting with mandated price lists, weak resale arbitrage, and durable legacy brands. In a source-audited Greater Austin-area panel, 60 percent of brand-years are exactly uniform for direct cremation and immediate burial and 49 percent for the basic-services fee. Sister branches are much closer in price than unrelated firms, yet their nonzero gaps are economically meaningful. Branch deviations have annual lag correlations of 0.90--0.95, and non-tied branch orderings are preserved in 98--100 percent of adjacent comparisons. Greater Kansas City supplies independent dynamic validation. In 2020, 13 SCI/Dignity locations occupy exactly three complete price vectors; a fourteenth shares the high tier for two services but differs for direct cremation. Detailed 2009 and 2016 tables show that the tiers arise from a few localized components layered over many exactly common prices. Across matched 2016--2023 branches, standard-funeral ranks are persistent; all 13 branches in the three core 2020 vectors remain in the 2023 survey, and every one receives the same $190 direct-cremation increase and the same $500 immediate-burial increase without losing its tier. An unpublished 2025 collection workbook identifies shared GPL documents spanning multiple branches. A model of a common component base, a finite menu of sticky tier vectors, and endogenous document scope rationalizes exact equality, selective localization, and additive common updates. The evidence qualifies, rather than overturns, uniform-pricing results: centralized decision authority need not produce a uniform price outcome.

detail.abstract: When retailers began selling caskets at a fraction of funeral-home prices, Service Corporation International (SCI), the largest U.S. funeral chain, announced that it would shift its pricing from merchandise toward services. Because the Federal Trade Commission's Funeral Rule bars a fee for using an outside casket, any price recaptured through services is paid by every family that buys those services, including families who buy the casket elsewhere. I trace the repricing through annual consumer-group price surveys of 21 Greater Austin pricing schedules from 1999 to 2011, four of them SCI-owned, audited cell by cell against the printed tables, and through matched Kansas City schedules from 2004 and 2007. Each Austin SCI schedule adopted a common menu in one of two January waves, 2006 or 2007. In its adoption year, its 18-gauge casket fell by 0.678 log points relative to local schedules while the sum of its separately quoted embalming and basic-services charges rose by 0.271. Between January 2005 and January 2007, relative to local trends, the bill for a family that supplied its own casket rose by about $2,084, a funeral with the 18-gauge casket by about $794, and immediate burial fell by about $420. Casket and embalming prices became common across the four legacy schedules while basic-services fees diverged. The goods-down, services-up direction is already established; the contribution is its incidence across families and its implementation across a chain's schedules.

detail.abstract: Enron Corporation remains one of the most closely examined corporate failures in modern financial history, yet the numbers it reported in the years before its collapse looked, on their face, unremarkable, a company posting fast revenue growth and rising profits. This paper asks whether a closer reading of those same numbers, using standard financial statement analysis alongside the Beneish M-Score, would have surfaced warning signs earlier. Working only from Enron's own reported 1998-2000 financial statements, the analysis tracks how revenue, net income, margins, receivables, liquidity, and operating cash flow moved together or, more often, apart. Revenue rose from $31.260 billion in 1998 to $100.789 billion in 2000, an increase of approximately 222.6%, while net income grew only 39.3% over the same period, from $703 million to $979 million. Net profit margin fell from roughly 2.25% to 0.97%, and accounts receivable grew 404.7%, outpacing revenue growth and pushing receivables from 6.59% to 10.31% of sales. None of these patterns proves manipulation on its own. Taken together with the Beneish framework's role as a screening device rather than a verdict, they illustrate why relationships between accounts not headline growth figures-are where financial statement analysis earns its keep.

detail.abstract: Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) are foundational to climate change mitigation analysis, providing structured explorations of long-term mitigation scenarios. In response to longstanding concerns regarding credibility, recent years have seen the emergence of increasingly sophisticated practices for evaluating modelled scenarios. Τhe vetting process formalised in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) aimed to exclude from the assessment those scenarios inconsistent with observed global emissions and energy trends. Community practice since AR6 has extended scenario evaluation well beyond this remit: more variables, regional scales, and forward-looking feasibility and plausibility checks. These developments have strengthened the scrutiny scenario ensembles receive, yet validation, vetting, feasibility, plausibility, and quality control are increasingly invoked interchangeably, despite distinct lineages, mechanisms and purposes. This short communication argues that such conflation, and the combination of checks without transparency about their respective aims, risks undermining both the evaluation process and, ultimately, the curated ensemble itself. Forward-looking checks warrant particular care since, unlike checks against observed data, no empirical ground truth exists, and benchmarks may evolve with evidence and expectations. Tying ensemble inclusion to such evolving benchmarks risks narrowing the exploratory scenario space toward futures that conform to prevailing expectations. We therefore propose a taxonomy that formalises these distinctions and recasts vetting as an inclusion decision that may draw on validation, feasibility, or plausibility but is distinct from each. We argue that evaluation should be indexed to scenario purpose: scenarios that diverge from such expectations may be precisely those that provide valuable insights into transformative change, emerging constraints, and alternative futures.

detail.abstract: BackgroundHearKids (SRESHT) is a clinically validated mHealth-based pediatric hearing screener developed to improve access to early hearing screening in rural communities with minimal training for grassroots workers. It includes behavioral observation audiometry (BOA), speech spectrum awareness task (SSAT), and speech recognition task (SRT) based screening modules for age-appropriate screening of children aged 0–6 years. The current study evaluated the acceptance, usability, and field validity of HearKids (SRESHT) among trained grassroots workers as a scalable tool for community-based pediatric hearing screening.MethodThe study was conducted in two phases in rural South India. In Phase 1, usability and acceptance of HearKids (SRESHT) among grassroots workers were evaluated using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) framework. In Phase 2, for field validation, trained grassroots workers performed HearKids screening on children (0 to 6 years of age) using age-appropriate modules, and results were compared with reference-standard DPOAE screening by an audiologist. Children who obtained a refer result on DPOAE underwent detailed tele-ABR to identify hearing loss.ResultsAmong 46 grassroots workers, UTAUT findings indicated positive acceptance and usability, with scores of 85% for performance expectancy, 75% for effort expectancy, 80% for facilitating conditions, and 78% for behavioural intention to continue use. Field validation included 135 children aged 0-6 years; BOA for 30 children, SSAT for 53 children/106 ears, and SRT for 52 children/104 ears. Ear based SSAT showed sensitivity of 90.00% and specificity of 95.83%; ear-based SRT showed sensitivity of 87.50% and specificity of 84.38%. As BOA screening was conducted in a free field, individual-based analysis showed sensitivity of 66.67% and specificity of 96.30%.ConclusionHence, HearKids (SRESHT) was acceptable, usable, and field-valid for pediatric hearing screening by trained grassroots workers in real-world settings and can serve as a scalable mHealth tool for pediatric hearing care in underserved communities.

detail.abstract: Decentralised finance data presents a distinctive paradox: while every data point is publicly recorded and accessible, deriving meaningful insights is obscured by the scale, fragmentation and complexity of the ecosystem. Key metrics illustrate that the rapidly evolving DeFi ecosystem introduces unique challenges for economic and financial research in accurately capturing financial activity in DeFi. These challenges stem from protocol architecture and the technical execution of transactions that complicate deriving economic meaning. Leveraging blockchain data for Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron, the paper illustrates three structural sources of measurement divergences: (1) the economically meaningful aggregation of Bitcoin transaction values, (2) the challenge of programmability and proliferation of spurious smart contracts and (3) comparability of use cases across different chains, exemplified by stablecoins. While the examples relate to specific chains and layers of technical execution, the measurement challenges generalise to all blockchains and DeFi ecosystems relying on a similar technical underpinning. We propose measurement approaches based on granular, databounded estimates that incorporate explicit assumptions, technical classification and disaggregation to align technical execution with economic meaning. The paper demonstrates that, despite the transparency of public blockchains, widely used indicators of cryptoasset and DeFi activity are highly dependent on methodological choices and underlying assumptions that warrant careful interpretation. The findings imply that on-chain indicators should be treated as noisy approximations rather than direct measures of economic activity.

detail.abstract: Accounting research has long centered on executives and directors as drivers of the corporate information environment; recent work considers the rank-and-file employees who also drive it. We survey the growing literature at the intersection of corporate disclosure and labor economics, organizing our discussion around the dual role of workers as both producers and users of corporate information. We introduce a Labor Life Cycle (LLC) framework that follows the employee through four stages: Human Capital Development, Search and Matching, Employment and Productivity, and Turnover and Retirement. At each stage, we first outline the principal theories from labor economics where information frictions are central and identify the reporting and disclosure institutions those theories leave unmodeled. We continue with a discussion of the empirical findings from accounting research that speak to key information problems at each stage, and close by highlighting the open questions where accounting researchers are well positioned to further contribute. Three themes emerge from our review. First, as producers, rank-and-file labor shapes the corporate information environment. In particular, the abilities, incentives, and job stability of the workers who produce accounting information are first-order determinants of reporting and audit quality. Second, financial reporting shapes the labor market: as users, employees use corporate disclosures in their search, bargaining, and departure decisions. Third, the theory implies a feedback loop between disclosure and employment, yet direct empirical evidence on the loop is scant.

detail.abstract: Background and Objectives:,To develop and validate a Hemodynamic-Aware Continuous-Time Transformer Network (HACT-Net) for predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in breast cancer using dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), and to evaluate its robustness against inconsistent acquisition protocols and missing temporal phases.,Methods:,In this retrospective multiCenter study, 894 breast cancer patients from three institutions were enrolled (Center 1: n=257, Center 2: n=356, Center 3: n=281). HACT-Net incorporated actual acquisition second embeddings, a time-intensity curve (TIC)-guided temporal aggregation module, and a masking mechanism to handle variable and incomplete temporal phases. Model discrimination was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).,Results:,HACT-Net achieved an AUC of 0.914 (95% CI: 0.856–0.962) on the multiCenter internal test set and 0.828 (95% CI: 0.770–0.880) on the independent external cohort, outperforming conventional fusion models (AUCs: 0.746–0.871).
