detail.abstract: This paper studies how housing supply constraints shape intergenerational educational mobility through house-price capitalization. Using the 2015 Chinese Census and 2016 China Migrants Dynamic Survey, I document asymmetric effects of housing-price appreciation: a 10% increase raises upward mobility among children in low-educated native homeowner households by 1.9 percentage points, reduces net migration of low-educated parents by 2.3 points, and increases parent-child separation among low-educated migrant families by 3.5 points. I develop a quantitative spatial model linking housing wealth, migration, family arrangements, education investment, and school access. Counterfactuals show that more elastic housing supply mainly redistributes the gains from urban growth, while equalising migrant children's school access raises aggregate upward mobility by 0.18 percentage points.

detail.abstract: Local projections (LPs) have become a standard tool for estimating dynamic effects in macroeconomics and are typically implemented using ordinary least squares (OLS) for a given lag order. We propose an alternative approach that exploits additional lags as excluded instrumental variables (IVs). Under a finite-order model with martingale-difference shocks, the resulting (optimally weighted) IV estimator is never asymptotically less efficient than OLS and, as we show, can deliver substantial efficiency gains when data are persistent. For the unit-root AR(1) data with i.i.d. errors, our baseline IV estimator (with one overidentifying restriction) has asymptotic variance 2h-1 , compared with h, the asymptotic variance of the OLS lag-augmented estimator in Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021), for an integer propagation horizon h. We then develop IV-based LP inference that is robust to unknown persistence and moderate local model misspecification, whereas the recursive VAR-based inference is generally not robust to the latter. We also characterize the trade-off between the degree of misspecification and the number of additional lag controls. Through simulations and an empirical application, we demonstrate that the proposed method can yield meaningfully shorter confidence intervals for impulse responses than OLS in finite samples.

detail.abstract: Dynamic pricing is a fundamental challenge in e-commerce since firms are required to balance maximizing revenue with consumer heterogeneity across international markets. Advances in digital technologies have allowed businesses to adopt more data-driven approaches in order to optimize their pricing strategies. This study proposes a consumer digital twin framework combining RFM behavioral segmentation with gradient boosting demand estimation to generate personalized pricing recommendations. Using the UCI Online Retail II dataset (803,459 transactions from 39 countries) combined with World Bank GDP per capita data, we find four moderately differentiated consumer segments and estimate price elasticity for each segment. Three pricing strategies (static, elasticity-based, and digital twins) are simulated on 5859 customers. We utilize a Monte Carlo simulation to validate results and conduct three methodological analyses: theoretical justification for pricing under inelastic demand, decomposition of revenue gains into inflation and personalization effects, and synthetic validation across a range of imposed elasticity values. The digital twin model yields a 59.62% increase in revenue over static pricing where 62.6% is attributable to personalization. Furthermore, synthetic validation reveals an important boundary condition: model recommendations degrade under elastic demand unless trained on data with genuine price variation. These findings demonstrate that the integration of simulation-based personalization in enterprise pricing regimes can improve profitability and ROI without sacrificing customer satisfaction.

detail.abstract: Most individual stocks underperform the index over long horizons even though the index is nothing but a portfolio of those stocks. We show that a one-factor lognor mal model under the physical measure, with the risk premium explicitly retained, isolates the mechanism: relative to a diversified benchmark, a stock’s log-wealth carries a drift penalty equal to one half of its idiosyncratic variance, 1 2σ2 ε. The sys tematic component of variance drag and the equity risk premium are of the same order of magnitude, but both are shared with the benchmark and cancel for a unit beta stock; the idiosyncratic component is not compensated by any premium and does not cancel. The probability that a stock outperforms the benchmark over a horizon T is 1 − Φ(1 2σε √T), independent of the risk premium and of the level of expected returns. With a single parameter, σε ≈ 0.35, the model reproduces the order of magnitude and the horizon dependence of the fraction of U.S. stocks that beat the market (about one third over five years, one fifth over twenty), the median stock’s shortfall, and, once the risk premium is reinstated, the fact that more than half of all stocks fail to beat Treasury bills. Because the penalty is idiosyncratic, it is diversifiable: for an equally weighted portfolio of K stocks it falls as 1/K and the outperformance probability converges to one half, so a portfolio that replicates the benchmark faces no headwind. For diversified active funds the same arithmetic shows that variance drag from active risk is second order relative to fees; the struc tural headwind documented here is a property of concentrated positions, not of active management as such.

detail.abstract: This paper updates the long-run implications of anthropogenic global warming seen in Graves (2017) as unfolding across two distinct "eras." Over the next half-century to century, continued (if decelerating) population growth, rising income, population aging, and expanding international trade are likely to interact with a warming climate to produce a period of substantial economic and environmental risk. Should humanity navigate that period successfully, the same forces plausibly reverse: population growth ends and then declines, rising income increases the demand for environmental quality, and the infrastructure built to accommodate a larger population becomes a source of abundance once population contracts. This update reiterates the competing worldviews of environmental "pessimists" and "optimists," situates each within this two-era framework using updated demographic and economic projections, and considers two conceptual arguments-the Porter Hypothesis and portfolio theory applied to environmental assets-that bear on how the transition between the two eras might unfold. Relative to the assessment of a decade ago, updated demographic, consumption, and emissions projections tilt the balance of evidence modestly toward the optimists, both in the ultimate severity of warming and in the timing of the second era's arrival.

detail.abstract: Mathematics learning difficulties constitute a condition in which students encounter various obstacles during the learning process, particularly in comprehending concepts, symbols, principles, and information, performing calculations, selecting problem-solving strategies, and applying mathematical knowledge to resolve problems. These difficulties are not solely indicated by low learning outcomes but are also manifested through the obstacles that emerge throughout the learning process. This study aims to examine the internal and external factors contributing to mathematics learning difficulties, as well as the identification, diagnosis, and remediation efforts. A literature review was employed by analyzing various relevant previous studies. The findings indicate that internal factors encompass the understanding of mathematical concepts, interest and motivation to learn, learning discipline and concentration, learning styles and attitudes toward mathematics, selfconfidence and mathematics anxiety, and study habits. Meanwhile, external factors include the family environment, the school environment and instructional processes, teacher competence and roles, instructional media and learning resources, and the peer environment. Identification and diagnosis of learning difficulties can be conducted through observation, analysis of student work, tests, error analysis, and interviews, so that the assistance provided corresponds to the difficulties experienced. Remediation efforts may be implemented through remedial instruction, the utilization of instructional media, guidance in learning, and the creation of a conducive learning environment. The implication of this study is that teachers need to comprehend mathematics learning difficulties comprehensively by considering both internal and external factors to design appropriate instructional strategies and assistance tailored to students' needs.

Recalculating indicator scales after a geographic filter, for example, can change the ordering of locations whose values have not changed. We examined how a diabetes-prevention planning dashboard could keep these comparisons consistent, show uncertainty in selection, and preserve a record of each decision. Methods. A self-contained prototype combined fixed-reference scoring, exact interval rank bounds, and reproducible exports. Controlled tests used 800 artificial landscapes, filtering and rounding experiments, and independent implementations. A separate application linked the uploaded 2025 PLACES county file to nationwide 2022 SVI rankings by five-digit county identifiers. Counties without diabetes estimates were excluded rather than imputed. The existing scoring rule was applied without refitting. Results. The real-data application retained 2,956 counties; 187 Kentucky and Pennsylvania counties lacked diabetes estimates, and one SVI county was absent from PLACES. At equal emphasis and a capacity of 30 counties, all nominal selections had uncertain membership within the supplied interval product: 183 counties were ambiguous, none was guaranteed selected, and 2,773 were guaranteed excluded. State-specific rescaling changed 27 of 49 retained-state top-ten selections, whereas fixed-reference scoring preserved all corresponding comparisons. Python and JavaScript agreed across 69 real-data configurations; 17 additional browser checks passed. The earlier synthetic experiments independently established the calculations' behavior under controlled inputs. Conclusions. Public county estimates can be incorporated without obscuring missing coverage, measurement periods, or ranking uncertainty. The real-data application demonstrates an executable analytical workflow, not validated prevention effectiveness. Its interval statements are conditional on supplied limits and a fixed SVI ranking; they are not simultaneous confidence claims or clinical recommendations.

title: Multi-Factor Timing：A Dynamic Strategy Selection Framework Based on Historical Strategy Performance
affiliations: and University of Geneva

detail.title: Multi-Factor Timing：A Dynamic Strategy Selection Framework Based on Historical Strategy Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it did not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Recent advances in quantitative investing have produced increasingly sophisticated multi-factor investment strategies. However, relatively little attention has been devoted to how investors should dynamically manage these completed strategies after portfolio construction. This study proposes a Multi-Factor Timing framework that treats complete investment strategies, rather than individual factors, as the object of dynamic selection. Instead of modifying factor definitions or portfolio-construction methodologies, the proposed framework dynamically allocates capital among competing multi-factor strategies according to their historical performance.

Using quarterly data from the Chinese A-share market, a fixed library of 242 candidate strategies is first constructed from five widely used equity factors using a continuous signed-weight design. Nine dynamic strategy-selection designs are then developed by jointly considering three decision dimensions: implementation delay, historical evaluation window, and portfolio breadth. Portfolio performance is evaluated using annualized return, annualized volatility, maximum drawdown (MDD), and the Sharpe ratio. Formal statistical inference is subsequently conducted for return, risk adjusted performance, volatility, and drawdown to evaluate the robustness of the empirical findings. 

The common-sample comparison reveals that the effects of selection lag and historical window length depend on the performance measure and portfolio breadth. The delayed designs generally have higher descriptive Top returns than their immediate counterparts, but paired tests do not establish significant improvements in mean Top or spread returns. Extending the evaluation window to four quarters raises the compounded annualized spread return at breadth 5 but lowers it at breadths 10 and 20 relative to the corresponding delayed one-quarter designs. Among the nine designs, D7 has the highest compounded spread return and spread Sharpe ratio and the smallest spread maximum drawdown in the common sample; D9 has the lowest spread volatility. 

Estimated mean Top–Bottom spreads are positive across the nine designs. Under the individual one-sided Newey–West tests, statistically significant positive mean spreads are concentrated in D5–D9. These tests establish positive spreads within selected designs, whereas common-sample paired comparisons do not establish general improvements in mean spread returns between matched timing designs. Evidence for reductions in maximum drawdown is limited. 

Overall, the findings suggest that quantitative investing should be viewed as a two level decision process consisting of strategy generation and dynamic strategy management. The proposed Multi-Factor Timing framework complements conventional factor investing by introducing dynamic strategy management as a new layer of quantitative investment decision making, while the observed performance differences among timing designs remain primarily descriptive.

title: Making Innovation Cities Regional Hubs: Lessons from the Effects of Public Institution Relocation
affiliations: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade

detail.title: Making Innovation Cities Regional Hubs: Lessons from the Effects of Public Institution Relocation

affiliations.org_name: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade

detail.abstract:
This paper warns that building innovation cities and relocating public institutions risk delivering no more than a temporary boost to regional economies. In the mid-2010s, when relocations were at their peak, growth in the share of the population living in the Seoul Capital Area (SCA) slowed temporarily, but population inflows from the SCA to the innovation cities have effectively vanished after 2017.

The innovation cities began losing population on net in 2023, and from 2025 even inflows from within their own regions turned into net outflows. The first phase of public institution relocation did increase population and employment in the innovation cities, but its spillover effects were limited in both size and reach. Relocation mainly raised service-sector employment in the host areas, and its effects fell short of expectations, with spillovers concentrated within about ten kilometers (km) of the innovation cities.

In particular, the persistent net outflow of people moving for work after relocation was completed points to a shortage of firms offering good jobs in the innovation cities. The paper argues that developing the innovation cities requires a selective, concentrated approach to relocating public institutions, together with an effective long-term hub strategy that turns the cities’ existing assets into agglomeration economies.

Relocations should be concentrated in areas with good access to the infrastructure of metropolitan and other large cities, so as to magnify the spillovers and build hub cities capable of drawing population away from the SCA. Because lasting productivity gains depend on creating agglomeration economies, industrial policy tied to the physical and human infrastructure of the innovation cities should be used to stimulate production in the cities and their surrounding areas. Finally, making innovation city policy more effective and sustainable calls for a governance framework that encourages cooperation among ministries and between the central and local governments.

title: European Defence Dependence on The U.S. and Its Geoeconomic Implications towards European Single Defence Market
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB)

detail.title: European Defence Dependence on The U.S. and Its Geoeconomic Implications towards European Single Defence Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.ethicsApproval: no
declarations.funderStatement: no

detail.abstract: The extraterritoriality of U.S. export controls has become an increasingly important constraint on independent European defence-industrial cooperation, procurement, and technology transfers. Yet legal authority alone cannot explain why U.S. regulations are able to influence the decisions of governments and firms operating outside American jurisdiction. This article argues that the effectiveness of U.S. export controls depends on broader structures of technological and industrial dependence embedded within transatlantic defence-production networked relations. Drawing on geoeconomics, economic statecraft, and theories of structural power, it examines how U.S. technological centrality enables export controls to generate regulatory power beyond territory and how this influence has created tensions with European strategic autonomy and technological sovereignty. The article analyses the recent efforts of European single defense market-building are and will be under constraints by the extraterritorial application of U.S. export controls, as responses to these structural vulnerabilities. It argues that legal contestation has produced only limited results because it does not address the underlying dependencies that make export controls effective. European defence-market integration should therefore be understood not only as a project of defence-industrial modernisation, but also as an attempt to reduce external dependence and rebalance technological and industrial power within the transatlantic defence economy.

title: What Recedes and What Remains When Markets Go 24/7: Evidence from Bitcoin and Ether Futures
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: What Recedes and What Remains When Markets Go 24/7: Evidence from Bitcoin and Ether Futures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses market data only and involves no human participants.

detail.abstract:
When an exchange extends trading to 24/7, what recedes and what remains? We answer using CME Bitcoin and Ether futures, which did not trade over weekends while spot markets remained open, and CME's move to continuous trading in May 2026. Before the transition, the closed venue reopened onto a price already formed elsewhere: the first futures trade reflects about 94% of the weekend spot move, the futures price moves one-for-one with spot within a minute, and the pre-close basis carries through the closure.

What the closure produced was a burst at the reopen. First-minute volume is four times the per-minute average over the following hour, compared with 1.6 times after the daily one-hour break. Only after weekends does the futures price range exceed the contemporaneous spot range: by about 20 bp on transaction prices and, once the book is rebuilt, by about 8 bp in Bitcoin and 13 bp in Ether on midquotes sampled at fixed intervals so that the measure does not depend on the number of trades.

The burst leaves no persistent price component. Order imbalance and the futures-minus-spot price change move together during the first seconds, but imbalance measured over those seconds does not predict the remainder of the minute or the following hour; the first-trade deviation largely reverses within five minutes; liquidity suppliers earn no larger realized spreads after weekends; and a contrarian strategy earns no statistically significant net profit after costs. After the transition, the futures-specific excess variation fell sharply in both contracts and was no longer detected in post-rebuild midquotes.

What remained was the trading clock. With no closure left to reopen from, the 17:00 CT minute on Sunday still carried 5.8 times the per-minute average volume of the surrounding hour, compared with 11.3 times before the transition. This spike was 3.1 times as large as the corresponding spike in spot and showed no fading over the weeks observed. E-mini S&P 500, euro FX, and Treasury futures, which retained their weekend closures, reopen in the same minute with volume spikes of roughly six to seven times.

The closure produced the reopening variation; the shared trading clock produced the concentration. Removing the closure took the variation away, but traders still crowded into the same Sunday minute.

title: Adaptive L-Statistic Tests for High-Dimensional Factor Pricing Models
affiliations: Nankai University, Southeast University and Nankai University

detail.title: Adaptive L-Statistic Tests for High-Dimensional Factor Pricing Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: This paper considers testing whether all alphas are zero in high-dimensional linear factor pricing models. Since the power of existing tests depends on the sparsity of the alternative, we construct a family of L-statistics by summing different numbers of the largest squared t-statistics for individual alphas. We then combine the corresponding p-values using the Cauchy method to obtain an adaptive test without specifying the number of nonzero alphas. We derive the limiting null distributions for sums involving a fixed number or a fixed proportion of assets and characterize their power under sparse alternatives and alternatives with individually weak signals. We establish residual multiplier bootstrap validity for fixed-order and proportional-order component tests and assess the adaptive combination numerically. Simulation studies compare the finite-sample size and power with existing alpha tests. Two applications to stock returns from China and the United States illustrate the proposed method.

title: Mathematics Anxiety in Learning: A Review of Characteristics, Contributing Factors, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies
affiliations: IAIN Syekh Nurjati Cirebon and IAIN Syekh Nurjati Cirebon

detail.title: Mathematics Anxiety in Learning: A Review of Characteristics, Contributing Factors, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this literature review as it did not involve human or animal participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Mathematics anxiety is a significant psychological phenomenon influencing students' affective, cognitive, physiological, and behavioral responses to mathematical content. This study examines the concept and characteristics of mathematics anxiety, its contributing factors, impacts on learning, position as a problematics in mathematics instruction, and strategies for its alleviation and prevention. Employing a literature review approach, this study synthesizes theoretical and empirical findings from prior investigations across educational levels. The findings indicate that mathematics anxiety manifests as fear, worry, tension, or discomfort when students face mathematics-related activities, including instruction, task completion, examinations, and everyday application. Its characteristics encompass cognitive, affective, physiological, and behavioral aspects. Contributing factors are classified into internal factors-psychological and cognitive conditions such as self-confidence, motivation, attention, readiness, perceptions, and learning difficulties-and external factors, including family, school, teachers' teaching styles and methods, material characteristics, and social environment. Mathematics anxiety potentially disrupts concentration, reduces self-confidence and readiness, impedes conceptual understanding and problem-solving, and affects engagement and achievement. Therefore, effective strategies are required, comprising student-centered learning, information and communication technology and instructional media, contextual approaches, scaffolding, positive teacherstudent communication, and self-regulated learning development. This study implies that mathematics anxiety should be recognized as a multidimensional problematics demanding attention to students' emotional conditions, appropriate instructional design, and teacher support in creating a supportive learning environment.

title: Measuring Normative Force, Not Topic Coverage: A Citation-Grounded Method for Assessing AI Governance Provisions in National Policy Documents
affiliations: VIT Bhopal University

detail.title: Measuring Normative Force, Not Topic Coverage: A Citation-Grounded Method for Assessing AI Governance Provisions in National Policy Documents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. The author designed and developed Meridian, the open-source method evaluated in this paper, and has no financial interest in it.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: National AI policy documents are often compared by what they mention. A strategy that names transparency, fairness and accountability looks complete, even if no sentence in it requires anyone to do anything. This paper asks whether a reproducible, citation-grounded procedure can separate what a policy document mentions from what it requires. We describe Meridian, a method that reads every operative sentence of a supplied document set and places it on a five-step normative-force ladder (aspirational, intentional, assigned, obligatory, enforceable), based on its addressee, modal force and any attached consequence. Two indices are kept apart: breadth, the share of 45 expected governance mechanisms a document establishes, and force, the share of those mechanisms carried by binding provisions. Verdicts are computed by rules; a language model writes explanations, and every citation is checked against the source text. We apply the method to stored analyses of 18 instruments from eight jurisdictions: China, Egypt, the European Union, India, Japan, Kenya, Rwanda and the United Kingdom. Breadth and force diverge sharply. Egypt's guidelines reach 84 per cent breadth with no binding mechanism, while China's measures reach 18 per cent breadth with three-quarters of it binding. No jurisdiction binds any environmental-sustainability mechanism. Checking the verdicts against the documents shows errors in both directions: rights-conferring and passive-voice statutory duties are under-read, and "must"-heavy guidance and translated legal idioms are over-read. The method is an early prototype; it has not been validated by legal experts, and the sample is small and exploratory.

title: The Revolving Door: Aging, Sorting, and the Illusion of Wage Convergence
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Revolving Door: Aging, Sorting, and the Illusion of Wage Convergence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

affiliations.org_name: University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics

detail.abstract: The classical Roback (1982) spatial-equilibrium model predicts that variation in amenities across locations is capitalized into some combination of local wages and rents, with the split governed by whether the amenity matters to firms as well as to households. This paper shows that the split also depends on who is doing the bidding for local housing. When a location's marginal home buyer is a household whose income is not tied to the local labor market-a retiree living on pensions and savings, or, increasingly, a remote worker paid by a firm located elsewhere-that household's bid for housing need not be offset by a lower local wage, so more of the location's amenity value is capitalized into rents and less into wages. As the U.S. population ages and remote work expands, this reallocates amenity compensation away from wages, producing what looks like regional wage convergence even though nothing has happened to the value of local amenities or to the classical arbitrage motive for migration. Applying the identical logic to skill rather than labor-force status implies that low-skill workers who remain in high-amenity locations to service high-income residents can receive a wage premium rather than the wage discount a single-type compensating-differentials model predicts. Because the households that trigger these price changes differ from the households displaced by them, the model also reproduces the long-noted empirical regularity that gross in-and out-migration are both high in high-amenity locations-a pattern earlier work, reasoning from a single-type model, read as evidence of costly or mistaken ("inefficient") mobility. We derive three propositions from a common bid-rent framework and sketch an empirical strategy for testing them with publicly available regional data.

title: Navigating the Complexity of Mathematics Instruction: A Systematic Review of Problems, Determinants, and Innovations
affiliations: IAIN Syekh Nurjati Cirebon and IAIN Syekh Nurjati Cirebon

detail.title: Navigating the Complexity of Mathematics Instruction: A Systematic Review of Problems, Determinants, and Innovations

detail.abstract: This study examines the problems, challenges, and innovations associated with strategies and methods in mathematics instruction. Mathematics is characterized by abstract concepts arranged hierarchically, requiring systematic and stage-by-stage learning. Consequently, the selection of appropriate instructional strategies and methods becomes a critical determinant of instructional effectiveness. This literature review synthesizes theoretical perspectives and empirical findings regarding the nature of strategies and methods in mathematics education, the factors influencing their selection, the problems encountered in their implementation, their impact on learning outcomes, and potential solutions. The review reveals that strategies constitute general plans for organizing instruction, while methods represent more specific ways of delivering learning activities. Their selection is influenced by content characteristics, student characteristics, learning objectives, teacher competence, media availability, learning environment, and time allocation. However, implementation frequently faces problems such as student ability gaps, misalignment between methods and objectives or content, low participation and motivation, limited instructional time, and inadequate classroom management. These problems contribute to learning difficulties, low problem-solving ability, mathematics anxiety, and declining learning outcomes. To address these issues, the study highlights identifying learning needs, selecting appropriate strategies and methods, implementing innovative models such as problem-based, project-based, discovery, and cooperative learning, integrating STEM and STEAM approaches, and utilizing media and technology.

affiliations: IAIN Syekh Nurjati Cirebon and IAIN Syekh Nurjati Cirebon

detail.abstract: This study examines the problems encountered in mathematics learning across three instructional modes: online learning, blended learning, and distance learning. Mathematics learning demands intensive communication because students must not only obtain correct answers but also understand concepts, procedures, and problemsolving steps. Using a literature review approach, this study synthesizes findings from various empirical studies to identify and categorize the key problems in mathematics education within digital learning environments. The analysis reveals seven major categories of problems: limited interaction and communication; inadequate digital literacy and technological infrastructure; low student motivation, concentration, and learning independence; the abstract nature of mathematical concepts; difficulties in understanding word problems and mathematical modeling; teachers' difficulties in designing integrated instruction and assessment; and challenges in monitoring student progress. Furthermore, this study discusses the impact of these problems on students' mathematical competence, influenced by cognitive and affective factors such as self-concept, anxiety, interest, and learning motivation. Finally, the study outlines strategies for addressing these problems in the digital era, including interactive digital teaching materials, game-based and STEMoriented e-books, augmented reality media, learning management systems, and formative and CIPP-based evaluation. These findings suggest that effective mathematics learning in digital settings requires systematic instructional design, adequate technological support, and sustained teacher training to ensure meaningful and equitable learning outcomes.

title: A Novel Learning-Based Model for Rheumatoid Arthritis Prediction Using MRI Images
affiliations: Bannari Amman Institute of Technology and Coimbatore Institute of Technology

detail.title: A Novel Learning-Based Model for Rheumatoid Arthritis Prediction Using MRI Images

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The dataset samples are acquired from the online open access repository which does not require any ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disorder that progressively damages joints, making early diagnosis essential for timely therapeutic intervention and improved patient outcomes. This study proposes a novel deep learning-based framework for accurate prediction and early diagnosis of RA using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. A consistency-based deep learning framework was developed by integrating an output normalization strategy, modified self-supervised pre-training, label-consistency learning, and a Residual GoogleNet (RGNet) architecture with residual learning and attention mechanisms. The proposed model was trained and validated using 5,945 MRI scans collected from 2,151 participants over a 10-year clinical study, comprising healthy controls, clinically suspect arthralgia (CSA), and early arthritis clinic (EAC) subjects. Comprehensive preprocessing, including artifact removal, intensity normalization, background thresholding, and anatomical slice selection, was performed to enhance feature extraction and improve learning robustness. The proposed RGNet framework demonstrated superior diagnostic performance, achieving an overall classification accuracy of 98.9%, an AUROC of 99.8% for RA prediction, and 98–100% AUROC across multiple RA classification tasks. Compared with conventional CNN, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Multilayer Perceptron, and K-Nearest Neighbor classifiers, the proposed model consistently produced higher sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value while significantly reducing false-positive and false-negative predictions. Furthermore, the lightweight residual architecture reduced computational complexity and completed network training in approximately 2 hours for MRI datasets while maintaining excellent generalization capability. The proposed RGNet-based consistency learning framework provides an efficient and reliable solution for automated rheumatoid arthritis prediction using MRI images. By combining advanced preprocessing, self-supervised representation learning, and multi-scale residual feature extraction, the model achieves state-of-the-art diagnostic accuracy and robustness, thereby supporting early clinical decision-making and facilitating the deployment of intelligent computer-aided diagnostic systems for rheumatoid arthritis screening.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Knowledge-Augmented Generation for Human-Supervised Curriculum Design
affiliations: Obuda University, TU Dresden and Karaganda Technical University

detail.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Knowledge-Augmented Generation for Human-Supervised Curriculum Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none.
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: none.

detail.abstract: Universities design curricula from programme goals, learning outcomes, courses, credits, and prerequisites. Regulatory requirements are also checked during curriculum design. We present Curriculum-KAG, a human-supervised decision-support prototype for curriculum design. It supports bachelor's, master's, and doctoral programmes. The proposed method combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Knowledge-Augmented Generation (KAG). It uses Kazakhstan's historical educational-programme corpus and multilingual retrieval. Contextual expert evidence is also incorporated into the process. A curriculum graph represents courses, prerequisites, and programme structures. Constrained semester planning is used to generate feasible curriculum plans. Archived pair-classification and ranking results are retained as separate experiments. Results from six programmes are also reported as a separate pilot study. An earlier engineering exercise produces 80 curriculum plans. Consultations with 28 experts provide additional contextual evidence. These results are reported with their respective evidentiary limitations. Neither study is treated as independent proof of academic quality. Course provenance is exposed for committee inspection and revision. Post-generation structural checks are also applied to proposed plans. The current evidence supports supervised institutional piloting of Curriculum-KAG.

title: The Wade Test: Generative AI and a CEO Bot
affiliations: Harvard University - Business School (HBS), University College London and Leiden University

detail.title: The Wade Test: Generative AI and a CEO Bot
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is transforming employees’ individual work, as well as their communication with other organizational actors. Increasingly, this communication is generated by AI bots, some of which are designed to mimic a specific individual. This study investigates whether Gen-AI can mimic a human CEO and whether employees display aversion to Gen-AI communication. We present a framework of Gen-AI aversion that distinguishes between a strong form (unrelated to Gen-AI’s performance) and a weak form (related to Gen-AI’s performance), and potential Gen-AI failures. In a field experiment with a firm, we extend the idea of a Turing test (i.e., a computer mimicking a person), to the idea of AI mimicking a specific person, namely the CEO. We call this the “Wade test” and assess if employees can distinguish between communication from their CEO and communication generated by an AI trained on the CEO’s prior communication. We find that responses are correctly identified 59% of the time, slightly better than random chance. When employees believe a response is AI generated, regardless of its actual source, they perceive it as less helpful. A second study with a general audience, using public statements from CEOs and from an AI intended to mimic those CEOs, finds that AI-labeled responses (irrespective of their actual source) are rated as less helpful. Taken together, our findings provide evidence of strong algorithm aversion to the use of Gen-AI in impersonating communication.

title: Human Development and Female Labour Force Participation: Evidence from 175 Countries
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Human Development and Female Labour Force Participation: Evidence from 175 Countries

detail.abstract: This study examines whether female labour force participation differs across levels of human development. Using a 2023 cross-section of 175 countries classified into Low (n = 25), Medium (n = 39), High (n = 44) and Very High (n = 67) human development groups, we compare participation measured by the World Bank World Development Indicators indicator SL.TLF.CACT.FE.ZS-labor force participation rate, female (% of female population ages 15+) (modeled ILO estimate)-based on International Labour Organization modelled estimates. Differences in group means are tested with a one-way analysis of variance, eta-squared, and Tukey honestly significant difference post-hoc comparisons. The pattern is nonmonotonic: the Low group shows the highest median (58.64%; M = 52.94%, SD = 22.99), the High group the lowest (median 46.90%; M = 45.52%, SD = 15.71), and the Very High group a higher centre (median 55.36%; M = 54.21%, SD = 8.07). The omnibus test rejects equality of means, F(3, 171) = 3.00, p = .032, η² = .05, indicating about 5% of total variation is associated with HDI-group membership. Only the Very High versus High difference is significant (mean difference = 8.69 percentage points, adjusted p = .020); all other pairwise comparisons are not significant. Because group variances differ substantially, a Welch heteroscedasticity-robust ANOVA and Games-Howell pairwise comparisons were also estimated as a robustness check; both confirm the primary result (Welch F(3, 61.56) = 3.84, p = .014; the same single significant High versus Very High contrast). The findings are consistent with a heterogeneous, contextdependent association plausibly reflecting informal work, structural transformation, and care and institutional constraints. Given the cross-sectional design, results are interpreted as associations, not causal effects.

title: The Value of Personalized Recommendations: Evidence from Netflix
affiliations: Netflix, Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management, Netflix, Netflix, Netflix and Cornell University - Cornell Tech NYC

detail.title: The Value of Personalized Recommendations: Evidence from Netflix

affiliations.org_name: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management

detail.abstract: Personalized recommendation systems shape much of user choice online, yet their targeted nature makes separating out the value of recommendation and the underlying goods challenging. We build a discrete-choice model that embeds recommendation-induced utility, low-rank heterogeneity, and flexible state dependence and apply the model to viewership data at Netflix. We identify recommendation-induced engagement from observational variation in algorithmic exposure, treating exposure as conditionally exogenous given observed user, good, and state characteristics. Separately, we estimate model-free diversion ratios from a randomized experiment that perturbs recommendations and use these to assess the validity of the structural model. We use the model to evaluate counterfactuals that quantify the incremental engagement generated by personalized recommendations. First, we show that replacing the current recommender system with a matrix factorization or popularity-based algorithm would lead to a 4% and 12% reduction in engagement, respectively, and decreased consumption diversity. Second, most of the consumption increase from recommendations comes from effective targeting, not mechanical exposure, with the largest gains for mid-popularity goods (as opposed to broadly appealing or very niche goods).

title: Redistribution with Unequal Life Expectancy
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Redistribution with Unequal Life Expectancy
detail.abstract: I study life-expectancy inequality in a Mirrleesian life-cycle framework with pension-linked fiscal externalities and private retirement saving. Heterogeneous longevity affects optimal redistribution by changing both the expected fiscal cost of pension benefits and the mapping from disposable income into social marginal welfare. I derive an ABCD optimal tax formula that incorporates these efficiency and equity effects. Calibrated to the U.S. economy, the model implies that accounting for heterogeneous longevity lowers optimal marginal tax rates, particularly at the bottom of the income distribution. These reductions generate welfare losses for the lowest-income types and welfare gains for most other earners, peaking at middle incomes.

title: Conducting Qualitative Interviews with AI
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management and NHH Norwegian School of Economics

detail.title: Conducting Qualitative Interviews with AI

affiliations.org_name: NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Economics

detail.abstract: Qualitative interviews offer rich insights into human behavior, but their lack of scalability has limited their use in economics. This paper introduces and evaluates AI-led interviews as a novel method for collecting qualitative data. Across different economic contexts, a comprehensive set of quality metrics demonstrates the high quality of AI-led interviews. We then demonstrate that AI-led interviews generate thematically richer responses than other survey methods for collecting qualitative data at scale. A decomposition exercise shows that the benefits of AI-led interviews mainly arise from asking dynamic probing questions. Importantly, AI-led interviews make themes visible that would otherwise be unobserved. These themes matter: We show that responses in AI-led interviews are internally valid and predict future behavior six months later. Finally, we demonstrate that AI-led interviews allow hypothesis generation about important economic phenomena, reaching thematic saturation in small samples comparable to studies using human-led interviews.

detail.abstract: How do production networks and market structure interact to shape the effects of trade and competition policy? We develop a model with two-sided firm heterogeneity, matching frictions, and imperfect supplier competition. More productive buyers match with more suppliers, inducing tougher supplier competition, lower input costs, and higher profits. Entry upstream thus benefits high-productivity buyers, while lower trade or matching costs favor mid-productivity buyers. Empirical evidence confirms that larger French and Chilean firms import higher quantities at lower prices as more Chinese suppliers enter, and that suppliers charge diversified buyers lower markups. We adapt methods for combinatorial, discrete-choice problems to estimate the model and perform counterfactuals. The interaction of endogenous networks and markups significantly amplifies the gains from policies that facilitate supplier entry or firm matching, and from deep trade agreements that combine tariff cuts with such policies. Fixed networks dampen while fixed markups amplify the gains from traditional tariff liberalization.

detail.abstract: Curricula are a critical site of cultural transmission, yet we know little about the values conveyed in textbooks across educational settings or the forces that shape them. We examine textbooks from Texas and California public schools and religious-private and home schools spanning 1980-2022, using computational and AI tools to measure presence and portrayal of people, topics, and values over time. Despite narratives of political polarization, Texas and California textbooks show substantial similarity. In contrast, religious private-school textbooks place greater emphasis on religious and character values and depict characters with lighter skin colors; we show these differences align with preferences and demographics of target markets. To explain public-school convergence, we develop a framework in which publishers serve a national market constrained by state standards and provide evidence consistent with cross-state spillovers in textbook content following standards revisions. Conversely, private-school publishers serve a more segmented, less regulated market, leading to greater differentiation.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how disruptions to local criminal governance affect adolescent fertility. We examine two episodes in Mexico: the militarized crackdown beginning in 2007 and the fentanyl-era territorial expansion of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel beginning in 2013. The first design compares municipalities where criminal organization was more deeply embedded before the crackdown with a low-exposure comparison group; the second exploits predetermined transport corridors associated with the later territorial reorganization. Conventional differencein-differences estimates imply increases of about 3.7 and 4.1 registered births per 1,000 females ages 10-19, respectively, and synthetic difference-indifferences estimates closely corroborate both effects. Organizational timing provides supporting evidence consistent with disruption, while descriptive accounting with recorded homicide measures leaves most of the fertility response unexplained. Survey evidence from ENDIREH shows larger increases in reported harassment among younger women, while a comparative corrido corpus documents more organized coercion alongside less frequent female narrative agency. Together, these findings show that changes in criminal authority can adversely affect young women's demographic and social outcomes in ways that homicide records alone fail to capture.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether food inflation operates as a transmission channel between water stress and poverty in highly water-stressed economies. Using annual country-level data for 2010-2024, the analysis applies a recursive dynamic panel framework estimated with two-step System GMM. The empirical strategy first evaluates whether water stress contributes to food inflation and then examines whether food inflation affects poverty after accounting for the direct role of water stress and selected macroeconomic factors. The findings indicate that higher water stress is associated with higher food inflation, supporting the view that pressure on freshwater resources can translate into food price pressures. Food inflation, in turn, is found to increase poverty, consistent with the welfare vulnerability of households exposed to rising food prices. However, water stress also remains relevant in the poverty equation, suggesting that food inflation is an important but not exclusive transmission channel. The results therefore support a partial mediation mechanism rather than a fully mediated relationship. From a policy perspective, the findings imply that poverty reduction in water-stressed economies should combine improved water management, stronger food-system resilience, and targeted social protection against food price shocks.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how government policies regarding tuition and university subsidies impact student enrollment and public university behavior. We study a system where the federal government sets domestic tuition and regulates institutions. Analyzing a 30-year period, we evaluate three major reforms: the 1997 introduction of increased, differentiated tuition; the 2005 implementation of field-specific subsidies; and the 2012 incentives for enrollment expansion. Combining empirical evidence with a theoretical framework, we demonstrate that long-run tuition increases can boost enrollment, though effects vary by field and university type. Specifically, while uniform tuition hikes reduce overall enrollment, differentiated tuition tied to expected educational returns increases enrollment, particularly at research intensive institutions. Furthermore, universities reallocate seats toward higher-tuition fields, creating notable substitution effects. Finally, although institutions have incentives to maximize revenue via international tuition, policies promoting domestic expansion effectively mitigate international enrollment growth. Our results underscore that accounting for institutional behavior is essential when evaluating higher education policies.

detail.abstract: An investor who acts on a return forecast chooses how much of it to use. From one identity for the certainty-equivalent loss in risk units we derive the price of every such choice. Each dimension of the forecast the investor acts on costs 1/T , the variance of an estimated Sharpe ratio, whatever signal it carries; each dimension in which he estimates the covariance matrix adds a Wishart factor that grows with the ratio of dimensions to observations. The familiar rules (plug-in, Kan-Zhou, Tu-Zhou, minimum variance, 1/N , decile sorts, parametric tilts) are fixed cells of the resulting grid. The cell that moves sets the number of rank groups from the forecast's information coefficient and holds 1/N when the forecast cannot rank. On a hundred large CRSP stocks with a machine-learning forecast it earns an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.2, against 0.6 for 1/N and 1.0 for the decile sort.

detail.title: A Theory of International Boycotts

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of international boycotts within a neoclassical trade framework. A coalition of households maximizes its own welfare subject to keeping the welfare of a foreign country below a tolerated level. I establish a general equivalence result: equilibria with such a boycotting coalition coincide with equilibria in which atomistic, price-taking boycotters maximize utility subject to fixed expenditure budgets on each country's goods and, equivalently, net spending budgets on each country's factor services. Optimal boycotts (i) take the form of prohibitions on importing foreign goods unless foreign comparative advantage is sufficiently large, and (ii) lead boycotters to increase their labor supply to spend more on domestic goods when income effects outweigh substitution effects. A boycott by all domestic households is equivalent to targeted import tariffs and to a voluntary export restriction by foreign firms covering the boycotted goods, and the optimal boycott mirrors the uniform structure of optimal import tariffs; however, the effectiveness of boycotts is diminished by leakage effects from nonboycotting households. Thus, while boycotts share key similarities with conventional trade policy instruments, they introduce complexities that position them as distinct tools of geoeconomic influence.

detail.abstract: This paper implements electricity spot pricing for Day-Ahead Market (DAM) on Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) using a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck jump-diffusion model based on Cartea-Figueroa framework. The spot prices are logarithmic and are decomposed into deterministic seasonal components which are represented by fourier series with a linear trend with stochastic mean-reverting residual augmented by Poisson jump processes. Model parameters are estimated using maximum likelihood on fifteen-minute Market Clearing Price (MCP) data. The analysis shows that the market is bounded above by an administrative price ceiling and below by a near zero solar surplus floor, introducing a deterministic, time-ofday censoring that is absorbed into the jump component. This drives the estimated jump intensity to the boundary of its interpretable region. The calibrate is therefore interpreted as an identification sensitivity analysis rather than a direct estimate of physical jump frequency. A likelihood ratio test reject the nested gaussian model and a normal probability analysis provide a before and after jump filtering result which confirms the departure from normality is because of the jump component. The results show that the regulatory constraints must be explicitly incorporated into stochastic price models for capped electricity markets such as the IEX, for providing important implications for model development, market analysis and the electricity price forecasting.

detail.abstract: Elected representatives have little incentive to pursue the interests of those electing them once they are elected. This well-known principal-agent problem leads, in a variety of theories of government, to non-optimally large levels of government expenditure. An implication is that budgetary rules are seen as necessary to constrain politicians' tax and spending behavior. Popular among such constraints are various Balanced Budget Amendment proposals. These approaches, however, are shown here to have serious limitations, including failure to address the central concern of spending level. An alternative approach is advanced here that relies on a Coase-like mechanism that transfers control of government spending to the voter. Prisoner's dilemma incentives and political competition are seen to be critical to the superiority of the present mechanism to approaches requiring budget balance. The adoption and enforcement of this mechanism are formalized here as, respectively, a one-shot game of political competition and a repeated game with reputational discipline: political parties that value future electoral success have a self-interested incentive to honor their spending pledges, so that credible restraint requires no outside enforcement beyond auditing and voter memory. Related literature on balanced-budget rules, alternative constraints on government spending, and the economics of rules, discretion, and reputation is also discussed.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper critically appraises the analytical advantages that artificial intelligence (AI), and generative large language models (LLMs) in particular, confer across three interlocking domains of contemporary digital finance: equity research, investment decisionmaking, and the emerging field of real-world asset (RWA) tokenization. 

Design/methodology/approach: Adopting a structured narrative-synthesis approach, the study integrates peer-reviewed empirical evidence on AI in equity markets with verified industry and preprint sources documenting the growth and technical architecture of RWA tokenization. Claims are tethered strictly to verifiable sources to avoid overstatement. 

Findings: AI delivers measurable advantages in information processing, predictive support, sentiment analysis, and accessibility for individual investors, while its integration into RWA tokenization enhances valuation, due diligence, risk assessment, and programmable automation. However, effects are heterogeneous and occasionally negative, and material regulatory and technical challenges remain in the tokenization domain. 

Originality/value: The paper bridges two literatures, AI-driven equity research and RWA tokenization, that are seldom appraised jointly, offering a disciplined, evidence-anchored assessment relevant to computer scientists, fintech engineers, and digital-finance scholars.

detail.abstract: Endometriosis is conventionally cited as affecting approximately 10% of reproductive-age women, yet that figure is drawn almost entirely from clinically diagnosed populations and functions as a structural floor rather than a verified population estimate. Selected laparoscopic series in women operated on for other indications have reported higher rates of visualized disease, and standard postoperative care leaves a long unobserved interval after the routine six-week visit; neither fact, by itself, measures hidden prevalence. This study used qualitative thematic analysis of publicly available, pseudonymous online material collected from 19 May 2026 through 16 September 2026—326 unique post titles from endometriosis communities and 550 one- and two-star reviews of a commercial menstrual tracking application, 500 of which disclosed location across 14 countries—to characterize what patients discuss about surgical and post-surgical experience and what low-rating reviews emphasize, without treating either corpus as an estimate of prevalence, recurrence, diagnostic delay, or market demand. Surgical or post-surgical experience was the largest coded title category (25%, n = 80); pain or acute flare appeared in 13% (n = 44), abnormal bleeding in 6% (n = 18), and explicit requests for peer validation in 5% (n = 17). Among low-rating reviews, complaints clustered on paywalls, subscription changes, and billing, and 72% of reviewers with disclosed location were outside the United States; because the review sample was restricted to one- and two-star ratings, monetization complaints are expected and cannot be read as evidence that users accept tracking and reject only commercial terms. The discourse is consistent with clinically salient events occurring between scheduled visits and with patients seeking peer interpretation in the absence of a personal longitudinal baseline. Those patterns identify a measurement gap; they do not fill it.

title: The Holy Creditor: Lending by Buddhist Temples in Pre-modern China

detail.title: The Holy Creditor: Lending by Buddhist Temples in Pre-modern China

detail.abstract: Between the seventh and tenth centuries, Buddhism spread from India into China, bringing with it not only religious teachings but also economic practices that were subsequently absorbed and localized. Buddhist temples in China thus became the country's earliest financial intermediaries, operating extensive lending businesses. This research traces that development through the case of Dunhuang in the ninth and tenth centuries, asking how temples first became involved in credit activities and how they organized capital, structured lending relationships, and managed risk as institutional lenders. The study draws on Dunhuang manuscripts held in the British Library, including contracts, ledgers, and temple annual reports recovered from the Mogao Caves, which together provide a rare, transaction-level record of monastic lending in practice. Three findings emerge. First, unlike other world religions, Chinese Buddhism developed doctrinal justifications for commercial lending, allowing temples to charge market rates of roughly 50% semi-annually and 100% annually without doctrinal conflict. Second, temples lent widely to peasants, officials, and merchants, earning profit margins of 20-100% that rose with borrower risk and fell as collateral quality improved, while managing risk effectively: default rates averaged 35%, well below the 55% market average. Temples also lent to one another to manage liquidity, revealing an interbank-style system of financial intermediation resembling modern banking practices. Finally, temple lending's eventual decline stemmed not from market failure but from state intervention. Together, these findings reposition Buddhist temples as sophisticated financial institutions central in premodern China.

detail.title: Growing with greener pastures: Examining the effect of educated politicians on forest cover in India

affiliations.org_name: Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS), Hyderabad Campus

detail.abstract: Forests are vital for environmental and health benefits, making forest management a top priority for policymakers. Using datasets that combine remote sensing forest data and temporal state assembly election, we investigate the role of educated politicians in promoting the growth of forest cover in India. We employ regression discontinuity design using close elections between graduate (with a bachelor’s degree or higher) and non-graduate politicians to tease out the causal effects. We find that constituencies that electing a graduate politician is associated with higher annual growth in forest cover relative to constituencies that barely elect a non-graduate politician. The result is robust to alternative bandwidths, specifications, education thresholds, outlier treatment, and alternative data sources, including district-level administrative and other satellite-based data. While exploring the potential reasons, we find multiple evidence to suggest that rising domestic demand for forest products, driven by economic growth, may create incentives for educated politicians to promote forest growth. First, we find forest cover to be positively associated with subsequent local economic activity and constituencies led by educated politicians to experience higher growth. Second, the effect of educated politicians on forest growth is found to be stronger in areas with greater pre-existing economic activity and greater intensity of forest-related industries. Third, these effects are particularly pronounced among younger politicians, consistent with the longer time horizon associated with investments in forest resources and growth. Finally, districts governed by a larger share of educated politicians exhibit greater value added in forest-related firms and increased employment in forest-related industries.

detail.abstract: Human rights practice is nearly universal in institutional form yet contested in philosophical justification. This article asks why human beings should have rights and contends that the question is usually treated as one question when it is at least three: a grounding question (why human beings are the kind of beings to whom rights are owed), a specification question (why these rights, with this content) and an allocation question (who bears the corresponding duties). Using philosophical-jurisprudential analysis, supplemented by a purposive comparison of adjudication in Germany, South Africa, Brazil and the European Court of Human Rights, the article reviews natural-rights, Kantian, agency-based, interest-based, capability-based, political and sceptical accounts and shows that no single-source theory performs all three tasks. It defends a dual-ground thesis: human rights are justified by the conjunction of a generic interest in leading a life of one's own and a standing, structural vulnerability to organised social power. The conjunction explains the addressees, urgency and equality of human rights, and it accommodates persons with impaired agency through a status-based rather than exercise-based reading of the first ground. Dignity is analysed as the name of the resulting status and as a constraint on permissible treatment, not as an independent premise. The article then confronts the strongest objection, the practice-based claim that philosophical grounding is dispensable, and identifies conditions that would falsify or narrow the thesis. It closes with an interpretive proposal for courts and rights scholarship. The contribution is conceptual and normative; the article reports no empirical findings. detail.abstract: Differences in factual beliefs between members of opposing political parties are sometimes attributed to politically motivated reasoning-an asymmetric reaction to information whereby congenial political messages are weighed more heavily. Using a series of survey experiments, we find that these underlying differences in factual beliefs are exaggerated, and that despite the expectations of both the general population and academic experts, US partisans show almost no politically motivated reasoning on the aggregate. What motivated reasoning we do find is asymmetric across parties, more prevalent among the affectively polarized, and most relevant to issues partisans consider important. Our  results suggest politically motivated reasoning is unlikely to explain the partisan belief gap. Our experimental design stands out in that it includes easy to understand informative signals, and a direct measure of belief movement in a non-binary environment. Our results suggest that whatever differences in beliefs exist among US partisans originate elsewhere.

detail.abstract: Renewable-hydrogen announcements continue to outpace projects reaching financial close or operation. This study examines how technically feasible hydrogen projects become investable across export and domestic value-creation pathways. A structured qualitative documentary analysis is organised around three minimum conditions: revenue credibility, infrastructure-readiness credibility, and de-risking credibility. Four international project trajectories—NEOM, Kassø, Hyphen, and FlagshipONE—provide contrasting evidence on financial close, operation, project preparation, and market-formation failure, while Algeria is treated as a bounded application. The comparison shows that resource quality and policy ambition are insufficient without credible demand, coordinated infrastructure, and allocable risk. Algeria’s strategy, corridor development, investment guidance, pilot preparation, and human-capital initiatives indicate an enabling environment being assembled for bankable projects and hydrogen-based industrial value creation. Renewable-hydrogen bankability is therefore conceptualised as a policy-constructed, sequenced project-formation outcome that distinguishes strategic signalling from project-level commitments.

detail.abstract: This paper identifies AI news shocks from financial markets and traces their macroe-conomic effects in the United States and the euro area. We combine a daily equity factor based on differences in firms’ AI exposures with sign, magnitude, and narrative restrictions in a Bayesian VAR to isolate revisions in AI’s expected economic value. Monthly local projections reveal an investment-led adjustment in the US: capital-goods orders rise early and persistently, while aggregate activity responds more gradually and with greater uncertainty. Producer prices increase before consumer prices, and the expansion spreads from sectors closely connected to the AI production network to the broader economy. In the euro area, equity prices rise and the euro depreciates; import and energy costs feed into inflation before real activity strengthens. Inflation expectations and nominal rates also increase. The results highlight a monetary policy dilemma: financial spillovers and imported price pressures arrive before the broader productive gains from AI adoption.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how a climate-related reporting mandate and firms' perceptions of climate risks shape the sophistication of firms' climate-related management control systems (MCSs), how these systems relate to GHG emissions, and whether they moderate firms' responses to the reporting mandate. We exploit the introduction of the UK Companies Act 2006 (Strategic Report and Directors' Report) Regulations 2013, which mandated GHG emissions disclosure for UK listed firms, and use panel data from 2009-2016 from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). The CDP provides detailed firm-level information on all control types of a climate-related MCS and allows for a difference-indifferences comparison of UK firms with a control group of US firms. Our results show that the mandate significantly increased the sophistication of UK firms' climate-related MCSs relative to US firms. This effect is found for all control types except for governance controls. We also find that perceptions of climate-related risks shape firms' climaterelated MCSs in different ways. Furthermore, we find a robust negative association between the sophistication of climate-related MCSs and firms' GHG emissions intensity. However, in contrast to prior studies, we do not find evidence that the reporting mandate itself reduced emissions, nor that MCSs moderated any such effect.

title: Tier-Aggregated Lexicographic Priority with Satiation: Recursive Budgeting Demand, Identification, and Welfare

detail.title: Tier-Aggregated Lexicographic Priority with Satiation: Recursive Budgeting Demand, Identification, and Welfare

detail.abstract:
We develop a satiation-augmented tier-aggregated model in which the consumer has lexicographic priority over satiation-adjusted tiers: below satiation, higher tiers dominate; above satiation, the consumer is indifferent within the tier. Each tier collapses to a scalar functional with a satiation level, so the consumer exhausts income on Necessities only up to the price-dependent cost C_N(p_N), then on Conveniences, then on Refinements, and finally absorbs any residual income in a linear, non-satiating Money/Saving tier. Because money is non-satiating, the demand system exhausts income in every regime: p·x* + m* = Y. The resulting demand system is a recursive budgeting with satiation structure whose compensated Slutsky matrix is block diagonal and whose uncompensated Jacobian is lower block-triangular, delivering sharp zero compensated cross-tier restrictions as a theorem rather than an assumption. We derive closed-form thresholds for Cobb–Douglas and CES tier functionals, establish existence, compact-valuedness, upper hemi-continuity, integrability (on interior regimes), and Walras' law of the demand correspondence, prove asymptotic normality of the recursive estimator with a generated-regressor correction, and derive closed-form compensating and equivalent variation with a kink at the satiation threshold. We provide a nonparametric derivative test of the zero cross-price restrictions with the correct quadratic-form asymptotic distribution and a Vuong comparison with a finite-substitute CES benchmark, as well as with QUAIDS and EASI. An approximate equilibrium existence theorem for finite-grid economies is given with a self-contained fixed-point proof and a Shapley–Folkman bound on the distance to an exact equilibrium, together with uniqueness under a block-wise substitutes condition and the two welfare theorems.

All empirical results in this paper are synthetic. A Monte Carlo study and a numerical illustration calibrated to U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey moments are provided; no real CEX estimation is presented in this version. All empirical results test the joint hypothesis of lexicographic priority over satiation-adjusted tiers, scalar tier-aggregation with satiation, and the chosen parametric form.

detail.abstract: As global financial systems increasingly integrate environmental considerations into risk management frameworks, classical structural credit risk models must adapt to capture non-linear climate transition risks. This paper extends the classical Merton structural framework by introducing a climate-adjusted asset dynamics model that incorporates stochastic carbon policy shocks, technological disruption penalties, and green technological shift jump-diffusions. We formulate the stochastic differential equation governing firm asset value under transition pressure and derive closed-form approximations for distance-to-default (DD) and probability of default (P D). Utilizing a synthetic panel of high-and low-carbon emission firms across carbon price trajectories from $50/tCO 2 e to $200/tCO 2 e, we quantify the non-linear credit deterioration in carbon-intensive sectors. Our findings demonstrate that unadjusted classical Merton models underestimate default probabilities for high-emission firms by up to 340 basis points under aggressive transition scenarios. Finally, we propose a climate-adjusted credit risk framework to guide capital allocation, bank stress testing, and sustainable financial product engineering.

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital learning technologies is transforming educational practices, including early childhood education (ECE). Despite the increasing availability of AI-enabled and digital learning tools, their adoption within Malaysian ECE settings remains insufficiently understood. This study examines the factors influencing the adoption of AI and digital learning technologies among ECE providers and educators in Malaysia. Drawing on technology adoption perspectives, an integrated framework was developed incorporating perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, digital competence, AI literacy, organisational support, facilitating conditions, and perceived ethical concerns as determinants of technology adoption intention. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed, and data were collected from 314 ECE providers and educators in Malaysia using a structured questionnaire. The collected data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to assess the measurement model and examine the hypothesised relationships between the proposed constructs and technology adoption intention. The findings indicate that the adoption of AI and digital learning technologies is associated with technological perceptions, educators' digital and AI competencies, organisational support, facilitating conditions, and ethical considerations. The study contributes to the technology adoption literature by extending an integrated adoption framework to the Malaysian ECE context. Practically, the findings highlight the importance of strengthening educators' AI literacy and digital competence, providing appropriate technological infrastructure and organisational support, and establishing clear ethical guidelines for responsible AI use. The study provides implications for policymakers, ECE providers, educators, and teacher-training institutions seeking to facilitate effective, developmentally appropriate, and responsible integration of AI and digital learning technologies in Malaysian early childhood education.
