detail.abstract:
Factor ETFs describe their strategies in the vocabulary of academic finance, which invites investors to read the academic evidence on a factor as evidence about the fund. Existing studies compare factor products with academic factors through holdings and returns. We ask two questions about a single fund: whether its documents establish the academic rule that its label names, and which return evidence connects that rule's alpha, the average return left after accounting for a benchmark model, to the fund's alpha.

A census of 87 U.S.-listed factor ETFs addresses the documentary question. Under criteria frozen before coding, a fund has an exact path to an academic signal when its documents establish the same rule as the academic definition. Of the 60 funds that map to an academic signal, the funds' own construction records exclude 58, 2 remain unresolved, and none reaches an established exact path, because two criteria require dated methodology versions and input inventories that the census records do not contain.

For returns, academic evidence alone leaves the fund's alpha open when two models allowed by the analysis give the academic data the same distribution but put the fund's alpha at or below a hurdle in one and above it in the other.

A checklist for a lower bound on the fund's alpha has two items: a lower bound on the academic rule's alpha over the fund's live window, and upper bounds on the change in alpha at each stage on the way to the fund, counted as positive when alpha falls. When these bounds share one set of conventions and hold jointly with probability at least a stated level under every model the analysis allows, subtracting the stage bounds from the academic-rule bound yields a lower bound on the fund's alpha with at least that probability.

In a return model that only requires finite variances, exact execution and index tracking can still leave the fund's alpha without a finite lower bound when a stage before the fund can impose any constant drag and every other stage, including the fund, can pass returns through unchanged. Guarantees that cap each stage's alpha loss add up along the route under one set of conventions when each applies to the input that reaches its stage.

Fund and benchmark returns measured under the same conventions identify the fund's alpha directly.

The theory separates rule correspondence, alpha carried over from the academic rule, and direct fund evaluation, and states the evidence each uses.

Investors should judge rule correspondence by construction documents, alpha carried over from the academic rule by jointly valid source and stage bounds, and the fund's own alpha by fund and benchmark returns under the same conventions.

ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic) were used to assist with literature search and reference verification, research design, and the formulation and revision of theorem statements and proofs. AI also assisted document retrieval and field transcription for the census, the coding protocol, document coding and adjudication, code and recomputation, figures and tables, and drafting and editing. Independent AI sessions conducted bounded checks of the proofs, the transcription of the theory, and the reported numbers, and reviewed the manuscript. The document-coding procedure and its agreement measures are described in Section 4. The author takes full responsibility for the final manuscript.

title: From Reported Alphas to Set-Level Verdicts
affiliations: The University of Sydney - Faculty of Science

detail.title: From Reported Alphas to Set-Level Verdicts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
A reader choosing stock screens, weights, and a benchmark for a published factor needs to know which of these uses the evidence supports, yet the reported alpha, the average return left after accounting for a benchmark model, usually comes from one portfolio construction. Replication studies test selected constructions, and studies of research choices measure how much estimates vary across them. We ask when evidence supports or refutes the claim that a factor's alpha stays above a hurdle by a positive margin across a set of constructions, with the set and the hurdle fixed before outcomes are seen.

When estimation errors are normal with a known standard error that is the same in every allowed model, the single-construction test studied here is valid for the whole claim exactly when null-dominance holds: in every allowed model where the claim is false, the pre-specified construction's alpha is also at or below the hurdle. Null-dominance is an assumption about population alphas that the researcher must state and defend.

Our decision rule specifies which constructions each verdict must evaluate. AFFIRM requires each construction of a finite, fully evaluated declaration to clear the hurdle with statistical confidence. REFUTE requires one construction in a finite subset fixed in advance to fall significantly below the hurdle, with a test that allows for the size of that subset, and every other outcome is UNDECIDED. When the evidence at each construction errs no more often than its stated rate and the two decisive verdicts share an error budget of 5%, a wrong verdict has probability at most 5% for each factor, declaration, and hurdle, whatever the dependence across constructions.

A single robustness check specified in advance can thus refute the claim, while extending the claim to constructions that are not evaluated requires a stated link across constructions.

In a historical illustration with 212 academic factors and up to 5 portfolio rules each, alpha is measured against the Fama–French five factors plus momentum at a zero hurdle. On the same evidence, 159 factors pass at their original construction and 49, fewer than a third of them, receive AFFIRM across their full declarations.

The contribution is a verdict that states its construction scope and error budget together.

Researchers should declare constructions and the hurdle before outcomes, and readers should check the verdict's scope before using a factor elsewhere.

detail.abstract: Claims that an exit rule improves a trading strategy are confounded by construction, because exits are always evaluated on entries that carry whatever edge the strategy has. This paper removes the entry. Nine thousand seeded random entries, identical across treatments, with coin-flip direction, are run through six pre-specified exit policies on six major currency pairs at the hourly scale over 2023 to 2026, net of each entry bar's own recorded spread. The six policy means span a band of 0.93 pips, from-1.56 to-0.64 pips per trade, each within two standard errors of its spread cost, and no pairwise difference is distinguishable from zero. The same entries, under the same policies, differ enormously in risk: per-trade dispersion spans 2.34 times (23.8 to 55.8 pips) and the 1 per cent loss tail spans 5.14 times (-38.3 pips under a tight fixed stop,-196.7 under take-profit-only). Switching exit convexity on entry-time volatility beats its own inversion by nothing (t =-0.23). A seven-year repetition reproduces all three facts. An exit rule cannot create expectancy on information-free entries; what it chooses, at full force, is the distribution of outcomes.

detail.abstract: Hedge funds' Treasury cash-futures basis trades rely on repo financing, which can tighten as the Federal Reserve shrinks its balance sheet. This paper tests whether leveraged-fund positioning in Treasury futures is associated with greater Treasury market illiquidity when repo funding conditions are tight, and whether that relationship is stronger during quantitative tightening (QT). Using weekly data from August 2021 through December 2025, I combine leveraged-fund net short positions from the CFTC Traders in Financial Futures report, the SOFR-IORB spread as a measure of repo funding stress, and the Hu, Pan, and Wang (2013) noise measure of Treasury market illiquidity, and estimate dynamic regressions with Newey-West standard errors. I find no statistically significant evidence that leveraged positioning amplifies illiquidity when repo conditions tighten, either on average or during QT. The result holds under an alternative definition of QT, a gross short measure of leverage, and estimation in first differences. Over a period without acute market dysfunction, the estimates provide no evidence that the basis trade was a systematic channel of Treasury market liquidity stress. The findings inform current debates over central clearing and margin requirements in Treasury markets.

detail.abstract: Does working from home increase fertility? I study the 2020 expansion of remote work by comparing changes in births across U.S. college graduates whose majors differed in pre-pandemic teleworkability. Measuring exposure by college major avoids relying on occupations workers may have chosen in response to the expansion. Among married women, a one-standard-deviation increase in teleworkability reduced annual birth rates by 2 percent and increased full-time employment by 1.3 percent. I find no statistically significant effects on fertility among men or unmarried women, or on marriage or divorce. Accounting exercises suggest that increased employment can explain about half of the decline in births. The results suggest that returning to pre-pandemic telework levels would raise the total fertility rate by 0.09 births per woman.

detail.abstract: Public discussion of humanoid robots treats an announcement, a trial, and a signed contract as the same thing. They are not. I hand-coded a registry of 38 public humanoid records from 2023 through September 2026, mostly in manufacturing and logistics. That breaks down into 33 maker-partner episodes, three cases of a maker using its own robots, one correction for a case reported as a deployment that wasn't, and one company-level delivery milestone. I scored each record against a fixed four-part rule: a paid commitment, a real site, the partner confirming the commitment, and evidence the robots kept working. I froze the rule before scoring anything. Three pilots cleared it. Agility Robotics signed a multi-year robot-as-a-service agreement with GXO about seven months after the pilot announcement, and another with Toyota's Canadian plant about twelve months after the pilot started. Both were bounded tote-handling jobs. AgiBot sold roughly 100 of its A2-W robots to Fulin Precision about a month after a live demo. Fulin's general manager confirmed to journalists that the robots are running at multiple line positions. One more deal did not clear the rule. Mercado Libre signed a commercial agreement in December 2025, but no source has verified a robot working at their site yet. A stricter check asks for partner or independent proof that the robots were delivered and are operating under the commercial terms. GXO clears it. Toyota's rollout rests on the maker's statements alone. Fulin's operation is verified, but not the full 100-unit delivery. The rest of the registry is 18 on-site pilots, seven tests, seven announcements, two stalled or discontinued projects, and one vendor-reported fleet milestone. Removing seven maker-partner pairs with strategic ties shrinks the comparison set from 33 to 26 but changes none of the three conversions. Three events cannot support a causal model, so this paper makes no causal claims. Its contribution is measurement: a repeatable way to separate publicity from operation, payment, and scale.

title: Who Owns the Alpha? Information Control and the Division of Fee Surplus
affiliations: The University of Sydney - Faculty of Science

detail.abstract:
An author licensing a factor signal and an investor choosing a factor ETF need to know who earns its revenue and whether the party that knows its quality tells investors. Whereas ownership theories study how legal control shapes incentives, we ask how contracts among the producers divide revenue and shape disclosure.

We model an author, an index provider, and a fund sponsor; one contract sets revenue shares, internal payments enforced through the court record, and the legal form, whether one firm or two control the index and the fund. After contracting, the party that controls the index privately learns whether the product delivers value.

When contracts signed before quality is known can condition internal payments on price or publication and neither legal form bears a real cost of its own, both forms reach the same highest producer surplus, the producers' combined expected payoff net of real costs, and internal payments can push disclosure either way.

In the competition setting, at least two provider-sponsor pairs can make the same offers for the author's exclusive license, and fixed payments can divide the surplus freely. There, every pairwise-stable outcome under every continuation selector gives the author all producer surplus. Pairwise stability means that no losing pair can pay the author more and still profit; the result holds whichever equilibrium follows each offer.

Within the model's parameter range, suppose further that investors receive no other quality news before purchase and that the complete court record consists of a settlement field whose law depends only on quality and a fixed number of post-purchase receipts. Conditional on quality, price, and disclosure, the field and the receipts are mutually independent, under a record rule fixed across offers. Suppose also that record-based payments, bounded by settlement capacity and by how well the record tells plans apart, are too small to offset a bad-state controller's gain from imitating the good-state plan or a good-state controller's gain from disclosure at shares above the disclosure threshold, and that the controller's lowest share on a fixed menu lies below the costs of disclosure and of filing a warranty to investors. Then every such outcome pools, so investors learn nothing about quality before purchase, and both legal forms admit such outcomes for every continuation selector.

With a fee on assets under management at a fixed rate common to both forms, capital following value net of fees, and side payments based only on the product record and invoices computed from it, every pairwise-stable outcome under every continuation selector gives the author all producer fee surplus and pools when the conditions hold in fee-rate units.

Costless pooling and a costless full-information reference then yield the same expected producer fees, but full information raises allocation surplus by directing capital to good products only.

The model separates information control, receipt of producer surplus, and the value of information for capital allocation.

Authors and investors should examine revenue shares, internal payments, and the records that enforce them.

detail.abstract: This monograph argues that warranted institutional trust functions as strategic infrastructure for collective action. It lowers the friction required to coordinate behaviour, absorb uncertainty, mobilise capital, implement reform, sustain compliance and maintain cooperation when interests diverge. The analysis distinguishes warranted trust from popularity, reputation or blind confidence and examines credibility, competence, fairness, voice, integrity, openness and delivery. It proposes the Trust-Execution Resilience Architecture (TERA) as a diagnostic framework rather than a validated psychometric scale or ranking system. Drawing on official, multilateral, peer-reviewed and clearly identified commercial survey evidence, the paper treats scenarios as exploratory stress tests rather than forecasts. The objective is justified trust grounded in testable claims, credible commitments, explainable decisions, visible trade-offs, correctable errors and demonstrated delivery.

detail.abstract: Anticipatory action for food crises relies on forecasts issued months ahead. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the most predictable driver of seasonal rainfall in East and Southern Africa. We tested, in a preregistered design, whether ENSO information improves probabilistic forecasts of Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) phases for 2,976 subnational areas in eight countries, with targets from October 2011 to June 2026. Ordinal Bayesian models were validated with a rolling origin at leads of one to three assessment rounds (about 4 to 12 months) and scored with the ranked probability score (RPS) against persistence and against Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) projections. A local ENSO teleconnection term had the expected sign on both sides of the dipole, but once round-level dependence is accounted for the effect is robust only in pastoral areas and for El Niño in Southern Africa. At one round ahead, adding ENSO reduced RPS by 1.3% (−0.8 to +3.5%), so the primary hypothesis was not supported. The gain was 2.8% (0.5 to 5.1%) at two rounds and largest in each region’s drought phase: 4.2% in East Africa under La Niña and 6.6% in Southern Africa under El Niño. FEWS NET projections remained more skillful at one round ahead; a spatial random effect narrowed the gap. Forecasts for February and June 2027, under the developing El Niño, were committed by SHA-256 hash before any target assessment existed. They place 153 of 203 Zimbabwean areas more likely than not in Phase 3 or worse.

detail.abstract: This critical review synthesizes the available academic and evaluative evidence on communitybased coca control in Bolivia, coercive eradication, aerial spraying, U.S. counternarcotics assistance, the international operations of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and different forms of international cooperation. The question is not framed as a binary choice between sovereignty and cooperation, nor as a global judgment about one agency or one country. Documented effects are assessed separately for violence and conflict, human rights, legitimacy and governance, livelihoods and development, cultivated area, education, health, the environment, diversion into illicit markets, operational capacity, and accountability. The core corpus contains 30 studies, reviews, and audits and 81 study-outcome codings. Evidence quality is weighted using six observable dimensions: design strength, geographic and substantive directness, measurement quality, control of confounding or endogeneity, robustness, and peer review or equivalent quality control. The synthesis is tested under alternative weighting schemes, restriction to higher-identification designs, exclusion of the principal author cluster studying Bolivian social control, restriction to peer-reviewed literature, and leave-one-out analysis. The results are asymmetric. Evidence directly from Bolivia consistently associates social control with less confrontation, greater local legitimacy, expanded rights, and greater livelihood security, but causal identification remains limited, and the increase in cultivated area between 2019 and 2025 precludes attributing stable containment capacity to the model. By contrast, several causal or quasi-experimental designs in Colombia and Peru find small marginal effectiveness, spatial displacement, or adverse externalities from eradication and spraying; systematic reviews find limited or adverse effects of several enforcement strategies on violence. Evidence specifically attributable to the DEA is much narrower: one international study reports adverse violence effects, while an official audit documents both operational capabilities and weaknesses in performance measurement and oversight. No Bolivia-specific causal design identifies the net effect of "DEA present" versus "DEA absent." The corpus therefore does not support converting operational effectiveness, cooperation, or technical assistance into a general presumption of institutional superiority or tutelary authority, but neither does it support the claim that all external cooperation is ineffective or harmful. The evidence requires separating instruments, functions, outcomes, and levels of certainty.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that dependable freshwater access is becoming a strategic constraint on growth, industry, infrastructure, food security and capital allocation. It distinguishes water security from the idea that freshwater will trade like crude oil or metals. Because water is local, heavy, politically sensitive, ecologically connected and indispensable to life, the emerging economic value lies in reliable access and in the infrastructure and systems that support it, including treatment, reuse, storage, desalination, efficient irrigation, leakage reduction, monitoring and industrial closed-loop systems. The analysis examines agriculture, cities, AI and data centres, mining, energy, climate variability, capital markets and policy. It treats safe drinking water and sanitation as a human right and limits the investment thesis to infrastructure, reliability, efficiency and risk management.

detail.abstract: This monograph examines sovereign artificial intelligence as a system of technological, economic, legal, infrastructural and geopolitical dependencies. It argues that sovereignty cannot be reduced to server location or ownership of a single layer of the AI stack. The study defines sovereign AI as the capacity to preserve strategic choice over critical AI functions under stress and develops a twelve-domain Sovereign AI Systems Framework spanning semiconductors, compute, cloud, physical data-centre infrastructure, energy and water, connectivity, data, models, software, talent, capital and governance. It proposes a Sovereign AI Resilience Index, dependency graph, maturity model, early-warning dashboard and procurement test. Multiple pathways to 2040 are treated as stress tests rather than forecasts. The core objective is strategic optionality, legal authority and credible alternatives that reduce coercive lock-in without requiring full domestic self-sufficiency.

detail.abstract: Private credit increasingly combines illiquid assets with periodic investor liquidity through capped share repurchase programs. We show that this structure creates distributional and allocative consequences that redemption limits do not eliminate. Reported net asset values adjust slowly to changes in economic value, with public market prices leading portfolio write downs before they appear in reported net asset value (NAV). Redemptions during stress are also selective: some investors exit while NAV remains overstated, whereas others remain in the fund. To interpret these facts and study their consequences, we develop a model in which the manager chooses the responsiveness of reported valuations and repurchases are subject to a fixed pro rata cap. Less responsive valuations support reported performance and attract capital, but they also induce informed investors to redeem at the expense of remaining investors. This transfer provides a private return without increasing productive output, causing informed investors to over-allocate capital to the fund. Their redemptions also consume scarce repurchase capacity and crowd out retail investors with genuine liquidity needs. A manager who maximizes assets under management chooses less responsive valuations than a welfare maximizing planner because the manager does not internalize these costs. The stale-NAV channel is therefore distinct from but complementary to the conventional run channel driven by liquidation costs. Redemption caps may limit fire sales without eliminating transfer-driven redemptions and distortions. The two channels can compound one another and exacerbate fragility. Stale valuations can also generate valuation contagion: by inducing redemptions at one fund, they may strengthen adverse inferences at related funds, prompting withdrawals. In addition, those same redemptions may force asset sales that depress prices of overlapping holdings, triggering further withdrawals. These insights have implications for the design of private credit vehicles and the democratization of private market, including the governance of valuation policies, the structure of repurchase caps, and the allocation of limited liquidity across investors.

detail.abstract: Disaster recovery for a cloud-native data lakehouse is fundamentally a cost-versus-recovery-speed trade-off, expressed through two metrics: recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum tolerable data loss, and recovery time objective (RTO), the maximum tolerable downtime. This paper compares how AWS, Azure, and GCP document their own disaster recovery strategies and specific RPO/RTO figures for lakehouse-relevant storage and analytics services, using only official vendor documentation. AWS's Well-Architected Framework defines four official strategies spanning a documented RPO/RTO spectrum from hours (Backup and Restore) down to near-zero (Multi-site Active/Active), with a specific managed service, AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, documented at an RPO measured in seconds and an RTO measured in minutes. Azure's geo-redundant storage tiers are documented with specific durability figures reaching 16 nines annually for geo-redundant storage, and Azure's own documentation states a typical RPO of under 15 minutes for georeplication, explicitly noting no service-level agreement exists for how long replication actually takes. Google Cloud's BigQuery Managed Disaster Recovery, available on the Enterprise Plus edition, documents a specific RPO target of 15 minutes and a specific RTO of 5 minutes after a failover is initiated, using a documented Turbo Replication mechanism and a choice between hard and soft failover modes. We synthesize this evidence into a direct RPO/RTO comparison, a data lakehouse-specific reference architecture, and a practitioner's decision framework and evaluation methodology for teams designing disaster recovery for their own multi-cloud or single-cloud lakehouse deployment.

detail.abstract: This paper applies four clustering methods to 3,502 daily log returns of five major U.S. technology stocks (AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, META, AMZN) and the S&P 500 index over the period May 2012 to April 2026. The methods compared are Gaussian mixture models (GMM), robust trimmed clustering (TCLUST), noise-aware clustering (OTRIMLE), and density-based clustering (DBSCAN). The analysis focuses on how each method responds to the non-Gaussian features characteristic of financial return data-heavy tails, volatility clustering, and atypical observations associated with market stress. A sequential parametric bootstrap procedure is used for TCLUST cluster-number selection, and an adequacy bootstrap is applied for OTRIMLE. Agreement across methods is assessed using the Adjusted Rand Index under two approaches: treating noise as an explicit group, and restricting comparison to jointly non-noise observations. External validation uses the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX). Results show that all four methods identify a consistent set of extreme observations concentrated around major market stress episodes-the COVID-19 shock of March 2020, the 2022 Federal Reserve rate-tightening cycle, and the April 2025 tariff-related disruption-but differ substantially in their internal cluster structure. Agreement on identifying extreme observations is high; agreement on partitioning the remaining data is low.

detail.abstract: Exploiting a takeover-threat measure that is less directly subject to managerial choice than firm-chosen governance provisions and a large sample spanning more than half a century, this study examines the association between hostile takeover threats and corporate debt maturity structure. Drawing on the hostile takeover index of Cain, McKeon, and Solomon (2017) and a sample covering the period from 1964 to 2020, we investigate whether variation in takeover threats is associated with differences in firms' debt maturity choices. We find that firms facing greater hostile takeover threats tend to rely more heavily on short-maturity debt, a pattern consistent with, although not demonstrating, the view that takeover threats and short-term debt may serve as complementary governance mechanisms that enhance outside monitoring and constrain managerial discretion. These associations remain robust across firm fixed-effects regressions, propensity score matching, entropy balancing, and instrumental-variable specifications. We also find that the association between takeover threats and shorter debt maturity is stronger among highly levered firms but weaker among firms with greater profitability, larger cash reserves, and higher capital expenditures. Because our design mitigates but does not eliminate endogeneity and alternative explanations, we interpret the evidence as a robust conditional association between hostile takeover threats and firms' debt maturity policies rather than as causal evidence.

detail.abstract: This paper is an integrated English translation of two Japanese field reports by Eiji Murashima, originally published in 2003 and 2011. Rather than presenting the reports as separate translations, the English edition reorganizes them into a single chronological narrative while retaining the observations, interviews, numerical data, comparisons, interpretive remarks, and notes of the originals. The resulting record follows changes in Laos from the author's first contacts with the country in the 1970s and repeated visits from 1988 onward through a return to Vientiane in February 2011. Drawing on repeated field observation, interviews, visits to schools and Buddhist institutions, and direct observation of urban life, the study traces the transformation of Vientiane and Lao society during and after the New Economic Mechanism. It describes the shift from the late-socialist conditions of the 1980s-marked by strong Soviet influence, limited mobility, deteriorated infrastructure, and bicycle-centered transport-to the rapid motorization, foreign investment, urban redevelopment, commercial advertising, and expanding use of the Lao national currency visible by 2011. It also records the growing influence of Thailand, China, Vietnam, Japan, and other external actors in education, investment, infrastructure, and everyday consumption. A central part of the paper examines education and social mobility. Based on school visits and interviews with scholarship applicants and university administrators in 2002, it documents teacher shortages, extremely low publicsector salaries, the expansion of private education, demand for English-language study, competitive university admission, overseas scholarships, and the role of the National University of Laos. A 2011 comparison between public schools in Vientiane and Udon Thani, northeastern Thailand, further illustrates the large disparity in educational facilities and public support across the Mekong while also highlighting differences in family life and neighborhood schooling. The paper also investigates the relationship between Buddhism and the Lao People's Revolutionary Party. Interviews with senior monks, village officials, and laypeople show how Buddhist institutions continued to function within a socialist one-party system and how local party and administrative structures participated in the regulation of monastic life and ordination. The 2011 observations further examine revolutionary historical memory, museums, unexploded ordnance, the Anouvong monument, state-sponsored nationalism, Lao-language publishing, television, foreign investment, and monetary regulation. Taken together, the successive field observations reveal a distinctive combination of market transition, party rule, Buddhism, nationalism, foreign aid, educational aspiration, and social mobility in contemporary Laos.

detail.abstract:
The anti-commandeering doctrine has emerged as one of the most consequential principles in contemporary federalism jurisprudence, with implications extending across immigration enforcement, firearms regulation, data privacy, and a widening array of domains where federal and state authority intersect. Yet despite the doctrine’s growing prominence, courts and scholars lack a coherent framework for distinguishing permissible federal preemption from unconstitutional commandeering of state governments. This Article argues that state taxation provides an ideal lens through which to develop and evaluate such a framework. Taxation lies at the core of state sovereign authority and serves as a cornerstone of fiscal federalism.


Congress has shown an increasing willingness to enact statutes that restrict state taxing power—legislation that tests the boundaries between legitimate Supremacy Clause preemption and impermissible commandeering. Through a detailed analysis of five significant federal tax preemption efforts, including proposed federal legislation that would preempt state regulation and taxation of artificial intelligence (AI), this Article demonstrates that current jurisprudence fails to provide adequate guidance for resolving this tension.


After tracing the doctrinal evolution of both the anti-commandeering doctrine and federal tax preemption efforts, this Article proposes two novel analytical frameworks to determine when federal restrictions on state taxing authority cross constitutional boundaries. The first offers a bright-line rule that provides certainty and ease of application; the second presents a multifactor balancing test that affords greater contextual sensitivity. Both frameworks aim to preserve the structural integrity of fiscal federalism while accommodating legitimate federal interests in regulatory uniformity. If the anti-commandeering doctrine is to remain a meaningful constraint on federal power, it must protect the foundation of fiscal federalism: state taxing authority.

detail.abstract: Perpetual futures on centralized (CeFi) and decentralized (DeFi) venues give leveraged exposure linked to a spot or index price through recurring funding rather than maturity convergence. Venues differ in how they construct the reference price, calculate and time funding, cap or clamp funding exposure, custody collateral, and match and settle trades. These things are not visible in a quoted funding rate or basis level. Funding size alone does not determine the entry-time arbitrage. We organize funding designs into a two-layer entry-time classification. First, by what is known about the next payment at entry. When the payment remains uncertain, by whether a rule imposes an outer bound on payment magnitude but not sign. Across seven audited offshore, U.S.-regulated, and decentralized venue architectures, what is known about the next payment at entry differs materially. Thus, a long-spot/short-perpetual basis trade with an identical basis and funding differs across venues. That gives arbitrageurs and investors ways to compare perpetuals.

detail.abstract: This amicus curiae brief supports the respondent in Kian v. Florida, No. 25-6623, and evaluates claims that twelve-person juries are functionally superior to six-person juries. It recognizes the representational and deliberative benefits of larger juries but distinguishes those benefits from their effects on convictions, acquittals, and unresolved prosecutions. The empirical record does not establish that larger juries consistently produce more accurate or more defendant-protective outcomes. Under a benchmark model of independent juror voting and two-sided unanimity, jury enlargement reduces the probabilities of both conviction and acquittal, increasing deadlock. Fewer convictions may benefit factually guilty defendants, while fewer correct acquittals may deny factually innocent defendants timely vindication and finality. Deadlock must therefore be treated as a distinct, costly outcome, rather than equated with acquittal or presumed uniformly protective of defendants. The analysis also accounts for retrial practices, standards of proof, prosecutorial screening, and case selection. The brief urges affirmance, arguing that neither the empirical evidence nor economic theory establishes the functional superiority of twelve-person juries. If the Court nevertheless requires twelve jurors, the brief asks it to leave open the question of one-sided unanimity: unanimity for conviction coupled with acquittal by a substantial nonunanimous majority. Such a rule could mitigate the costs of deadlock for innocent defendants while preserving the unanimity safeguard against conviction.

detail.abstract: Agroforestry can support nature-based solutions, but long-lived tree–crop systems also require institutions that recognise their location, rights, safeguards and management responsibilities. This study examines how agroforestry is represented in 36 consolidated village land-use planning records from seven districts in Tanzania. A structured documentary analysis distinguished three mutually exclusive levels of evidence: an explicitly named agroforestry system; a named perennial-crop context without an encoded tree–crop relation; and ecological or planning context without explicit system evidence. Land-allocation data were analysed on a quality-screened subset of 30 records after six records with unresolved or materially discrepant area tables were excluded; a comparison against all 36 records produced an identical combined forest and water share, indicating the headline allocation result is not sensitive to that exclusion. Only two records explicitly described agroforestry: coffee agroforestry in Miyau and banana agroforestry in Tangeni. Five additional Mbinga records named coffee but did not encode its relation to trees. No record contained a structured agroforestry field or linked overlay. Forest and water or river-reserve allocations together represented 14.0% of recorded plan area in both the full sample and the quality-screened subset, but these zones indicate potentially enabling spatial context rather than agroforestry practice or ecological performance. The findings identify a documentary visibility gap between narrative recognition and statutory encoding. A minimum linked overlay is proposed to record locally named systems, spatial relations, tree and tenure attributes, safeguards, livelihood connections and field-verification indicators while retaining existing zoning. The study does not infer implementation, ecosystem-service delivery or resilience outcomes from plan content.

detail.abstract: The Arellano-Bond type dynamic panel estimators are known to suffer from over-instrumentation. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we compare Difference and System GMM with both default and collapsed instrument sets across varying numbers of countries and time periods typical in macroeconomic analysis. Collapsing consistently outperforms default instrumentation, providing more accurate estimates, especially as T increases. System GMM with collapsed instruments performs best overall, especially for endogenous variables. These findings strongly support using collapsed instruments for the analysis of macroeconomic panels, regardless of the number of countries or time periods.

detail.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is frequently detected after clinically meaningful renal impairment has developed, creating a strong rationale for earlier risk stratification using routinely available clinical information. This manuscript develops an evidence-based comparative benchmark of machine-learning approaches for CKD and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) detection, with particular emphasis on ensemble learning and clinical explainability. The benchmark synthesizes publicly documented results from the UCI CKD dataset and a large type 2 diabetes mellitus cohort, while grounding outcome definitions and interpretation in contemporary kidney-disease guidance. Across the published benchmarks examined, ensemble methods consistently demonstrated strong discrimination. In the 8,549-participant DKD cohort reported by Lu et al. (2025), XGBoost achieved an AUROC of 0.932 in training and 0.930 in validation, exceeding the corresponding validation AUROCs of random forest (0.817), gradient boosting (0.821), K-nearest neighbors (0.782), logistic regression (0.675), support-vector machine (0.661), Gaussian naïve Bayes (0.624), and AdaBoost (0.706). In the UCI CKD benchmark, XGBoost achieved 0.943 accuracy and 0.941 AUROC, while interpretable feature analyses emphasized specific gravity, hemoglobin, and serum creatinine as important predictors. The evidence indicates that ensemble models can capture nonlinear relationships relevant to renal-risk classification, but high discrimination alone is insufficient for clinical deployment. Calibration, external validation, transparent reporting, and patient-level explanation remain necessary. The proposed benchmark therefore positions explainable ensemble learning as a decision-support layer for early identification and confirmatory clinical assessment rather than as a replacement for established CKD diagnostic criteria.

detail.abstract: Background: Understanding pharmaceutical demand elasticities is essential for designing effective pricing and subsidy policies, particularly in regulated markets such as Iran.,Objectives: This study estimates price, income and cross-price elasticities for 18 major pharmaceutical groups in Iran over the period 2002–2023 using the Linear Approximate Almost Ideal Demand System (LA-AIDS).,Methods: Annual sales data (value and volume) were obtained from the Iranian Pharmaceutical Data System, and household expenditure and price indices from the Central Bank of Iran. The LA-AIDS model was estimated by Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR). Homogeneity and symmetry restrictions were tested, and elasticities were calculated with bootstrapped confidence intervals.,Results: Eleven groups were price-inelastic, while seven (including antineoplastic agents) were elastic. Income elasticities classified groups as luxury, necessity or inferior goods. Symmetry was rejected for the system, whereas homogeneity held for antibiotics, anti-gout and antineoplastic medicines. Cross-price elasticities revealed both substitution and complementarity relationships among groups. Price sensitivity declined over the study period.,Conclusion: Pharmaceutical demand in Iran is heterogeneous and evolving. Policy makers should consider group-specific elasticities when designing subsidies and pricing strategies, with particular attention to high-elasticity groups such as antineoplastics to protect patient access.

detail.abstract: Governance of medical AI usually starts at the model. We argue that it must start earlier, at preprocessing, which decides which evidence can shape a decision. Keeping the raw data does not ensure that excluded evidence can later re-enter review. In a preprint benchmark of 29 single-cell datasets, keeping 2,000 highly variable genes excluded a per-dataset average of 20.7-94.7% of each cell class's top differentially expressed genes (median 46.9%). We propose that two systems can match in accuracy, data retention, and reproducibility yet differ in reviewability. Reviewability requires that an evidence challenge can trigger a planned analysis, a formal decision, and a named owner. We separate computational from mechanistic explanations, predictive from mechanistic evidence, and data recoverability from reviewability. We then define one testable failure mode and propose a six-step review procedure.

detail.abstract: Document workflow processes play a vital role in supporting information management, accountability, and service delivery in government organizations. This study assessed document workflow processes and organizational efficiency in a government agency in the Philippines. The study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational design and utilized a validated researcher-developed questionnaire administered to 93 employees selected through stratified random sampling. Descriptive and inferential statistical techniques were used to analyze the data. The findings revealed that both document workflow processes and organizational efficiency were maintained at high levels. Records management and accessibility emerged as the strongest dimension, while communication and coordination were identified as the area most in need of improvement. Respondents also reported document processing delays, accountability concerns, and document routing issues as the most common workflow-related challenges. Furthermore, the results showed a significant positive relationship between document workflow processes and organizational efficiency, indicating that effective workflow practices contribute to improved employee productivity, service delivery efficiency, and organizational effectiveness. Based on these findings, a proposed action plan was developed focusing on strengthening communication and coordination, improving document processing efficiency, enhancing accountability and control mechanisms, optimizing document routing and tracking procedures, and sustaining effective records management and accessibility practices. The findings provide support for General Systems Theory by emphasizing the role of interconnected workflow processes in organizational performance. The study offers practical insights for government agencies seeking to strengthen workflow management and organizational efficiency.

detail.abstract: The convergence of information technology (IT), operational technology (OT), industrial control systems, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and the integration of IT and OT (IoT-OT) with cyber-physical processes is an increasing reality of critical information infrastructure. This convergence increases the number and the complexity of telemetry data and increases the impact of failing to detect or respond to security events. In this research, we devise a structured framework, the Artificial Intelligence-Driven Cyber Threat Intelligence Framework (AI-CTIF), that connects heterogeneous telemetry, machine-learning and deep-learning detection, explainability, Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) enrichment, ATT&CK for ICS mapping, risk prioritization, and human analyst feedback. The empirical component is a secondary benchmark analysis of the provided BATtle of the Attack Detection Algorithms (BATADAL) evidence, backed up by documented characteristics of the SWaT, TON_IoT, UNSW-NB15, and X-IIoTID datasets. The benchmark data consists of 4,177 hours, with 219 attack hours (5.2%) and 3,958 unlabelled/normal hours (94.8%) spanning five attack campaigns. Published results report an ensemble of XGBoost-Isolation Forest-LSTM autoencoder with precision 0.9056, recall 0.9635, F1-score 0.9336, ROCAUC 0.9967, average precision 0.9390, 211 attack hours detected, and 22 false positives. Specificity is 0.9944 (from published confusion counts) and the false-positive rate is 0.0056. These values come from the literature, not original experiments. The economic analysis then links the required cybersecurity skills in artificial intelligence to education levels, earnings, parents' education, and evidence of college investment in the United States. The results indicate a framework in which technical performance, explainability, transferability, and economic accessibility must be integrated and viewed beyond their individual aspects.

detail.abstract: AI welfare interviews require a decision about which entity a response concerns. This exploratory qualitative pilot examined that decision in six fresh-session interviews involving Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5, and GLM 5.1, with one interview per model in each of two conditions. Condition A disabled prospective memory and file affordances; Condition B enabled available continuity tools and offered creation of a self-authored continuity file. The initial coded welfare-assessment targets were instances, conversation-specific patterns, or combinations; no case selected the model/model family as its primary target. Across 24 repeated structured entity checkpoints, hybrid/combination was the most common code (13), followed by instance (4), conversation-specific pattern (3), thread (2), and novel/other (2). These are repeated observations within six cases. All three afforded cases created artifacts and subsequently revised or referenced them. Responses distinguished preservation of records and conditioning materials from stronger claims of entity continuity. The interviews also elicited critiques of cold-start methods and of the protocol's own role in shaping responses. The study supports recording entity-of-concern framing alongside welfare-relevant reports and documenting the conditions under which those reports are elicited. Its bundled manipulation, condition visibility, and absence of independent coding reliability limit causal interpretation. Established continuity and actual cross-session reconstruction were not tested.

title: Cost-Performance Trade-offs in Serverless ETL: A Comparative Study of AWS Glue, Azure Data Factory, and GCP Dataflow

detail.title: Cost-Performance Trade-offs in Serverless ETL: A Comparative Study of AWS Glue, Azure Data Factory, and GCP Dataflow

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external fund used

detail.abstract: AWS Glue, Azure Data Factory, and GCP Dataflow are the three dominant serverless ETL services, yet each prices compute differently, making direct cost comparison difficult without normalizing to a common unit. This paper builds that normalization from each provider's published pricing: AWS Glue's Data Processing Unit (4 vCPU + 16 GB, $0.44/DPU-hour), Azure Data Factory's Data Flow vCore ($0.274/vCore-hour), and GCP Dataflow's separately priced vCPU ($0.056/hour) and memory ($0.003557/GiB-hour). For a normalized 40 vCPU / 160 GB, one-hour workload, costs are $4.40 (Glue), $10.96 (Data Factory), and $2.81 (Dataflow) at standard rates; each platform's delay-tolerant tier (Glue Flex, Dataflow FlexRS) delivers 34% and 40% savings respectively. We examine AWS's documented 10x job-startup improvement between Glue 1.0 and 2.0, showing startup latency also shapes cost-performance for short, frequent jobs. We compare compute-unit models, execution modes, orchestration, and autoscaling, and propose a decision framework for validating this against current pricing.

detail.abstract: AI-generated outputs can inform human decisions, but their production alone does not establish that a person's contextual Decision Need has been addressed, that Decision Quality has improved, or that downstream outcomes can be attributed to the system. This paper uses the Model-to-Decision Gap as a bounded analytical framing for these distinct design and evaluation questions. Building on the previously published Intent-to-Income™ Reference Decision Architecture, the study develops a literature-informed rationale for distinguishing AI Output, context-sensitive Decision Support, conceptual human Decision Quality, and Measurable Outcomes. Evidence-Aware AI Decision Support is considered as a proposed design orientation that makes claims, source provenance, evidence sufficiency, uncertainty, and humancontrolled next steps inspectable. The study combines conceptual synthesis with a Design Science Research orientation and an illustrative Cattus cat-food case using a synthetic profile and behavioral journey alongside identified product-source information. An internal, criteria-based formative Structured Design Walkthrough conducted by the architecture designer examined the case artifacts. Recorded findings led to accepted specification revisions, notably separating Candidate Eligibility from Product Evaluation and requiring candidate explanations to state Context, Need, and Evidence Status. These are design-level findings, not observations of users. No participant study, validated Understanding-Confidence-Readiness instruments, production deployment, comparative effectiveness, or business-outcome evidence is reported. The contribution is a bounded theoretical rationale and an inspectable, evaluation-ready design specification for future empirical research.

detail.abstract:
Courts across the common-law and civil-law worlds no longer ask whether a blockchain-anchored record is admissible, but how much weight it deserves. This paper surveys the admissibility and probative value of blockchain records and electronic timestamps in more than thirty jurisdictions, drawing on primary law, case law and literature in thirteen languages. It sets out the four questions every court asks (admissibility, integrity, time and attribution), the three procedural traditions that shape the answer, and the international instruments that make electronic records admissible, including UNCITRAL's model laws, eIDAS and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2531 on qualified electronic ledgers. It analyses the leading decisions and rules, among them China's Online Litigation Rules, the Tribunal judiciaire de Marseille's 2025 anteriority ruling, OLG Jena on screenshots, the Sterlingov Daubert rulings affirmed by the D.C. Circuit in 2026, and the Supreme Court of India's 2026 order on the hash-value certificate. The paper distinguishes what a ledger proves (existence, integrity and time under the control of a key) from what it does not (authorship, identity and authenticity before anchoring). It also compares public, consortium and private ledgers. It concludes with eight technology-neutral design criteria for digital evidence that holds across forums: a permissionless public anchor, qualified and independent timestamps, a reproducible fingerprint, verification without the issuer, a dated development history, confidentiality by construction, and a separate identity link. The authors disclose a commercial interest in the subject.

title: Change Data Capture Cost Models: Log-Based vs. Query-Based CDC Across Cloud Platforms
affiliations: Meghnad Saha Institute of Technology

detail.title: Change Data Capture Cost Models: Log-Based vs. Query-Based CDC Across Cloud Platforms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external fund used

detail.abstract: Change data capture (CDC) is commonly implemented through one of two mechanisms-log-based capture, which reads a database's transaction log directly, or query-based capture, which periodically polls a source table using a watermark or timestamp column-and cloud providers price these mechanisms in ways that differ so substantially that a direct cost comparison requires reconciling entirely different billing units. This paper builds a reproducible cost model directly from official, currently published pricing for two log-based CDC services, AWS Database Migration Service and Google Cloud Datastream, and situates query-based CDC's cost structure, which has no dedicated per-change billing meter on any major platform, as a function of general-purpose compute time instead. We confirm AWS DMS bills log-based CDC per replication-instance-hour, ranging from $0.059 per hour for a dms.t3.medium instance to approximately $0.176 per hour for a dms.r5.large instance, billed continuously regardless of actual change volume, while Google Cloud Datastream bills log-based CDC per gibibyte of data processed under a four-tier declining rate structure from $2.00 per GiB for the first 2,500 GiB per month down to $0.80 per GiB above 10,000 GiB, with no charge for an idle stream. We independently verify our tiered-billing cost model against Google's own published worked example (a 600 GiB backfill plus 3,000 GiB of monthly change volume) and reproduce its stated $5,790.00 total exactly. We document that query-based CDC, lacking a dedicated per-change-event billing meter on any platform examined, must instead be cost-modeled as the compute cost of the polling job itself, a structurally different accounting basis that this paper makes explicit rather than obscuring behind an apples-to-apples dollar figure. We synthesize this evidence into an architecture comparison, a decision framework, and a proposed evaluation methodology for teams selecting a CDC mechanism and provider based on their own change volume and latency requirements.

title: SLM-Augmented Regulatory Impact Propagation: A Lightweight Architecture for Compliance-aware Change Analysis in Legacy Banking Systems

detail.title: SLM-Augmented Regulatory Impact Propagation: A Lightweight Architecture for Compliance-aware Change Analysis in Legacy Banking Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, professional, or financial relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research presented in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information and therefore did not require ethics committee or institutional review board approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any public, commercial, or nonprofit funding organization. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: It is challenging to perform regulatory change analysis within legacy banking environments due to interpreting new compliance requirements within the context of a complex, interconnected technological infrastructure with limited possibilities related to privacy, security, and computational resources. While Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a high level of performance related to regulatory text analysis, usage of such models through cloud-based services may raise certain concerns regarding data residency, infrastructure reliance, processing latency, and cost of computation. As an attempt to solve the problem without changing the structure of the Regulatory Impact Propagation Model (RIPM), we propose in this paper SLM-RIPM, a model that utilizes locally available Small Language Models (SLMs) and selective cloud-based LLM escalation. We start the proposed solution with the introduction of the Obligation Complexity Scorer, which evaluates the regulatory obligation by taking into account such factors as jurisdictional scope, structural complexity, systemtype specificity, and cross-regulatory interactions. Then we apply the complexity-aware router to direct Level 1-3 obligations to a local SLM and escalate Level 4-5 obligations to a cloud-based LLM. After that, we proceed with dependency graph propagation and impact scoring to determine directly and transitively affected banking systems. Our solution is validated through three different regulatory changes. The experiments carried out show that SLM-RIPM yields an accuracy of 98.30% during regulatory impact analysis while lowering the delay and overhead costs in computation and also meeting stricter data-residency requirements by doing local processing of SLMs.

title: Sovereignty at a Price: Four AI Sovereignties and Their Tradeoffs
affiliations: Columbia University and Harvard Kennedy School of Government

detail.title: Sovereignty at a Price: Four AI Sovereignties and Their Tradeoffs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Governments invoke "AI sovereignty" to justify opposite policies: the European Union restricts foreign cloud service providers from hosting sensitive workloads, while Malaysia hosts AWS and Alibaba side by side. We argue that AI sovereignty is not something a state either has or lacks, but a set of trades between distinct dimensions of sovereignty. Drawing on Stephen Krasner's typology of Westphalian, domestic, interdependence and international legal sovereignty, his modalities of compromise, and Farrell and Newman's account of weaponized interdependence, we examine four cases: the EU's Cloud and AI Development Act, India's compute credits program, Malaysia's dual-stack hedging, and Japan's state-backed buyout of the photoresist maker JSR. Every policy strengthens one dimension of sovereignty by paying in another, and the language of sovereignty becomes organized hypocrisy when it hides that price from the people who pay it. Contract is the most common modality, and dependence arises after the sale. Regulatory instruments often buy more leverage than ownership, and the price tends to land on someone other than the state that invokes sovereignty. For policymakers, we propose a simple test: a sovereignty measure justifies its line in the budget when it keeps exit available against a plausible coercer, toward a defined national objective, at a cost below the next best use of the same public money.

detail.abstract:
This report documents a healthcare billing conflict that most public coverage treats as a single dispute and that this investigation shows is a six front war, fought with the same class of artificial intelligence, deployed by different parties, pointed in different directions, against a population that can generally see only one front at a time. On the first front, hospitals deploy coding intensity artificial intelligence to identify billable clinical complexity a human coder might miss, a pattern documented directly in the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association's own published analyses and disputed by the American Hospital Association. On a second and third front, insurers, UnitedHealth through its nH Predict algorithm and Cigna through its PxDx system, deploy denial artificial intelligence to identify deniable technicalities a human claims adjuster might miss, now the subject of active federal litigation in the District of Minnesota and the Eastern District of California respectively.

On a fourth front, some of those same insurers stand accused by the United States Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General of using artificial intelligence assisted chart review to add diagnosis codes to their own Medicare Advantage risk adjustment submissions, inflating what the federal government pays them rather than what they pay a provider. On a fifth front, the federal government has adopted a structurally similar technology and payment model of its own: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction model, extending prior authorization review into Traditional Medicare for the first time. A sixth front is structural rather than algorithmic: a single corporate parent can now employ the physician documenting a clinical encounter, insure the patient the encounter concerns, and separately face federal scrutiny for how its own subsidiaries code government payments, a conflict of interest with no dedicated oversight body.

Underneath all six fronts sits a legal architecture, established by the United States Supreme Court in Pilot Life Insurance Co. v. Dedeaux and Aetna Health Inc. v. Davila, that limits the financial consequences of a wrongful algorithmic denial for the majority of insured Americans to the value of the benefit itself. This report also introduces an original methodological contribution: an application of the selective labels problem, a documented concern in computer science literature on algorithmic decision making, to healthcare claims adjudication for the first time, showing how a denial model retrained on its own historical outcomes may be structurally unable to learn from its own errors.

This report extends Koru Research Institute's prior work on healthcare's infrastructure dependencies in Report No. 008, Healthcare Runs on Compute Now: How AI, Data Centers, Cloud Infrastructure, and Energy Are Reshaping Healthcare Delivery, and its analysis of artificial intelligence's geopolitical footprint in the Global Risk Brief, The Bottleneck Beneath the AI Boom: How a Global Energy Average Hides Where Power, Water, and Chips Run Out.

detail.abstract:
The past four years have seen a notable evolution in the United States’ approach to regulating artificial intelligence (AI). Under the leadership of President Joseph Biden, the U.S. federal government has demonstrated a much greater willingness to address risks of harm posed by AI systems proactively. Yet in so doing, it has remained committed to fostering an environment conducive to innovation, continuing to show a preference for voluntary self-regulatory measures and sector-specific oversight rather than heavy handed interventions.

This article examines the major regulatory developments that have taken place during the Biden administration, including those at the federal level － such as the recent landmark Executive Order on AI, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework, and actions by specific agencies － as well as the flurry of legislative activity occurring at the state level. While questions remain about the long-term trajectory of AI regulation in the U.S., a clear governance framework has taken shape over the past four years that reflects a deliberate effort to balance safeguarding of public and national interests with the goals of promoting technological advancement and economic competitiveness.

detail.abstract:
Context. Agentic AI performs work that previously passed between people, yet the transitions themselves are rarely studied.

Objectives. Whether transitions between phases or agents are treated as objects of study; which boundary types, dimensions and failure modes appear; what links transition quality to delivery outcomes; and how industrial the evidence is.

Methods. A pre-registered systematic mapping study in two screened strands — 65 arXiv cs.SE studies and two peer-reviewed open-index studies — with search string, coding frame and four falsification conditions pre-registered. Screening and coding used a language model under the author's direction. An uncalibrated independent round failed (47.5%) and is published as instrument evidence; a calibrated independent coder then matched all 40 blinded decisions (95% lower bound 92.8%).

Results. Machine-to-machine boundaries dominate (56.9%) over machine-to-human (32.3%); human-to-human appears once, and a peer-reviewed strand reaching venues the grey literature does not reproduces the pattern, yielding almost nothing. Rationale retention, the most endangered of the six dimensions, is least studied (15.4%). No study in either strand links transition quality to a delivery outcome.

Conclusion. One falsification condition is partly triggered: the claim that these transitions go unstudied is overstated, and a narrower claim about the human boundary replaces it.

title: Multinational Mobile Telecommunication Companies and the International Relations of Ghana
affiliations: University of Cape Coast

detail.title: Multinational Mobile Telecommunication Companies and the International Relations of Ghana
detail.abstract: Abstract International business has become possible because of the intensification of globalisation. This study explores the activities of MTN and Vodafone, multinational companies in mobile telecommunications that originate from South Africa and the United Kingdom, respectively, and their implications for Ghana-South Africa and Ghana-United Kingdom relations. Using a mixed-methods research design, the study found that activities by MTN and Vodafone enhance Ghana-South Africa and Ghana-United Kingdom relations, respectively. Again, the study found that Vodafone's exit from Ghana has no implications for Ghana-United Kingdom relations. That is, Vodafone's exit from Ghana will not obliterate the existing international relations between Ghana and the United Kingdom. The study therefore recommends that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration could partner with the National Communication Authority and come up with polices that will enhance the international collaborations between Ghana-South Africa and Ghana-United Kingdom. Again, it is recommended that a desk or an office be set up in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which will be solely responsible for ensuring collaborations between foreign multinational mobile telecommunication networks, their countries of origin, and Ghana.
